CHR, a declarative language optimized for pattern processing, features constraint heads that link an equation-free constraint phase with a predicate initiating a solution search. Its design is inspired by Prolog, with a distinction being that constraint phase predicates are only allowed once (as single head rules), drawing comparisons to logic programming and single-programming. Prior studies examining the computational power of CHR have primarily looked at multi-head rules. This study assesses the computational power of the CHR phase in the context of single-head rules, with key findings that include: (1) the addition of single-head rules does not enhance the computational power of a given problem; (2) if a single-head rule is possible, it will result in a corresponding single-head CHR constraint theory; (3) such theories are capable of solving complex problems through the use of auxiliary constraints; (4) the addition of such rules does not necessarily increase the number of such problems that can be solved by the underlying theory in a proportional manner to the number of added rules.

We have analyzed the orientation of galaxy spins across 1.3 million galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 12-3 and found that the large-scale arrangement of galaxy spin directions aligns in a consistent cosmic framework. Contrary to expectations, our findings indicate that the spin directions do not conform to any specific plane at the galaxy level. However, when galaxies are grouped into larger clusters, their spin directions collectively align with a common plane. This phenomenon holds true across various mass ranges for galaxies and suggests that the internal processes governing galaxy rotation play a significant role in shaping their orientation. Notably, the alignment of galaxy spin directions becomes more pronounced as galaxies are grouped at higher masses. This observation implies that the large-scale cosmic environment influences the galaxy distribution, possibly through the effects of gravitational forces that permeate through galaxy clusters.

The goal of meta-learning is to develop a generalized understanding that enables rapid adaptation to novel tasks using a small amount of data. Despite this goal, current meta-learning methods often struggle in few-shot learning scenarios due to local minima and overfitting issues. To address this challenge, we propose a straightforward training technique that utilizes multiple optimization steps to produce multiple solutions, effectively mitigating overfitting and improving the robustness of each learning module. Our method, known as module-based optimization, is applied to the MAML algorithm, resulting in a revised and enhanced algorithm called MB-MAML. The experiments demonstrate that MB-MAML outperforms its predecessor on multiple benchmarks for one-shot image classification, while offering a valuable insight into the behavior of meta-learning algorithms.

A brain disorder, multiple sclerosis, affects the brain in intricate ways.
Currently, the study of multiple sclerosis relies heavily on self-reported symptoms
which can be subjective. This study aims to explore the relationship between the
brain's structural changes and behavioral patterns in multiple sclerosis patients
by using a unique dataset. Firstly, we applied a technique to create detailed 3D
brain images from a set of MRI scans. Next, we used deep learning algorithms to
understand the different brain patterns in people with multiple sclerosis, and we
discovered that these patterns can be linked to specific clinical symptoms.
However, these patterns vary in intensity across the brain, and are often not
linked to the same clinical symptoms. This led us to investigate whether we could
find a way to summarize the brain's activity in an easier-to-understand way.
Through our analysis, we found that we can use a combination of brain patterns to
understand the brain's behavior in a more meaningful way. This new approach enables us
to identify patterns in the brain's activity, and to link these patterns to the
clinical symptoms that they are associated with. This new understanding of the brain's
activity, allows us to identify people with multiple sclerosis who exhibit
unusual symptoms, and to identify patterns in the brain's activity over time.
This could potentially help us to understand how multiple sclerosis affects the brain
in new ways.

Recent literature in AI Ethics explores the ethical considerations of AI systems in relation to their creators, users, and broader society. As this field advances, it is essential to map its developments to better understand its current status and future directions. Our study provides an extensive analysis of over 500 AI Ethics papers by utilizing natural language processing techniques to identify core themes. We discovered that these works can be broadly classified into three categories based on their primary focus: technical, conceptual, and applied AI Ethics. Our findings suggest that research in all categories has become increasingly diverse and sophisticated over time. We also created a detailed taxonomy comprising 25 key topics that categorize the discussions within these categories. This taxonomy serves as a valuable resource for both AI Ethics novices and experienced researchers.

We investigate expanded versions of monadic second-order logic on infinite words
and its capacity to express nonregular languages. The addition of a language with a
neutral letter to MSO leads to undecidability, but if the added letter is from MSO1, the
resulting logic becomes undecidable with infinite words as well. For ω-words defined on
topological spaces, which also fall under MSO1, our results show decidability thanks to
effective closure properties. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that quantifying the
infinitude of subwords in a given language can only be achieved through the addition of
a neutral letter in MSO.

In high-dimensional dynamic wireless networks, the escalating costs of channel estimation and the necessity for adaptable traffic management become significant issues, primarily due to the channel estimation and traffic characteristics that evolve rapidly. To mitigate these problems, we develop a hybrid traffic scheduling and channel estimation strategy that integrates the principles of multi-arm bandits into the traffic scheduling process, effectively minimizing channel estimation costs while aligning traffic allocation with channel usage patterns. This proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts traffic and channel assignment based on real-time observations, utilizing the Kalman filter for channel estimation and the generated data in the Kalman filter update. This approach enables the simultaneous optimization of channel estimation and traffic allocation, outperforming existing solutions in terms of both average and worst-case throughput-outage rates.

A comprehensive analysis of the semi-leptonic beta decay in nuclei has been conducted, focusing on the interaction between protons, neutrons, and electrons within a nuclear framework. The study utilizes a 5-dimensional approach to understand beta decay and incorporates the Skyrme nuclear potential to model the nuclear structure. The semi-leptonic beta decay is achieved by incorporating the Fermi-goldstone boson into the Skyrmer. The study utilizes the first principles to derive the matrix elements and extract the V_{ud} value from the analysis. The study also compares the V_{ud} values from different nuclei and finds a correlation between these values. The study provides an explanation of the correlation between these values and attributes it to the nuclear structure. The study provides an explanation of the nuclear structure and shows that the nuclear structure plays a significant role in the correlation between the V_{ud} values.

We introduce a fully-convolutional network tailored for image denoising tasks, 
featuring an architecture that efficiently leverages identity mappings to minimize 
computational costs and preserve essential low-frequency information crucial for 
accurate reconstruction.

In this research, we explore the application of multiview data representation for various purposes, including classification and clustering. We introduce the Shared Components of Private Latent Spaces (SCPLS) framework, which leverages the shared components within private latent spaces to capture the underlying structure of multiview data. Contrary to existing methods that often rely on the shared components among all views, we focus on exploiting the shared components between specific view types, leading to improved performance in classification and clustering tasks. The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on multiple multiview classification and clustering datasets.

We analyzed a dataset of 1033 low-redshift galaxies with unique near-infrared spectroscopic observations, and we used a combination of Bayesian stellar population analysis and stellar mass models to identify galaxies that deviate from the typical mass-stellar population relationship. These outliers were chosen based on a specific type of deviation that cannot be easily explained by galaxy mergers or interactions, and their unique spectra do not show signs of an additional ionized component. Compared to other types of active galaxies and normal galaxies, the red outliers have higher mass and older stellar populations, but their specific SED characteristics, including low dust content and non-stellar UV emission, are what truly set them apart. By examining the environments of the red outliers, it appears that they have similar surroundings as optically-selected AGN, but their physical conditions differ significantly, and their unique properties may indicate a new class of AGN or alternative black hole growth mechanisms.

As AI systems become increasingly integrated into human decision-making, the need to develop AI that can interpret and align with human moral values becomes more critical. A primary obstacle in addressing this issue lies in the fact that humans' moral judgments often appear inconsistent when viewed abstractly, making it difficult to establish a universal moral framework. Our research focuses on the concept of moral consistency through the lens of moral foundations theory, aiming to create a moral concept encyclopedia that can be used to teach AI systems to consider the moral implications of their actions. Our initial approach involves applying foundationalism, a philosophical framework that views morality as consisting of multiple, universal principles, to better understand the structure of moral reasoning. By analyzing the moral principles underlying diverse moral concepts, such as fairness, trustworthiness, and respect for community, through the perspective of multiple moral foundations, we can provide insights into the complex nature of morality. Our research contributes a moral knowledge base that can serve as a foundation for further studies in moral alignment and AI collaboration with humans.

A valuation ring embedded within a field is a ring where each element from the field resides within it. In this study, we identify and categorize valuation rings where every prime factor divides 2. We establish that the dual of an Alexander dual concept applies to these specific valuation rings. Additionally, we establish a connection between these valuation rings and certain types of matroids, along with providing some specific examples, such as the Fano matroid.

The proposal of quantum scarring has significantly impacted our understanding of quantum dynamics. Despite most research focusing on the area-preserving Frenkel-Hopf-Dirac Hamiltonian, it is also feasible to explore the two-dimensional Dirac equation as an alternative model for studying scarring and associated quantum phenomena. This study investigates the effects of a Gaussian perturbation to the Dirac Hamiltonian, demonstrating that the resulting model is analogous to the Frenkel-Hopf-Dirac Hamiltonian and subject to a similar diagonalization process. By employing a mapping between the two models and an analytical method, we derive an analytical expression for the scarred spectrum in the Gaussian perturbed Dirac equation. Furthermore, we apply this expression to calculate the spectral characteristics of quantum scarring in two-dimensional systems, and our findings are in line with both theoretical predictions and numerical analysis.

The integration of communication between vehicles has given rise to various advanced driving systems. This study examines two such systems in particular: Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control and Platooning, considering the distinct perspectives of individual drivers and the fleet operators. To assess the impact of these technologies on daily routes, a simplified model is proposed that accounts for the decision to adopt vehicle autonomy. A cost-benefit analysis is conducted based on the number of driven kilometers, the frequency of service and fuel consumption, while also taking into account the quality of service and comfort provided by autonomous vehicle services. A multi-criteria decision analysis is applied to compare the benefits of autonomous vehicle services under different scenarios.

To effectively counter the spread of misinformation on social media platforms, 
accurately identifying potential spreaders is a crucial first step. This study 
introduces a novel approach for assigning credibility scores to Twitter users, 
enabling the separation of users who can potentially disseminate false 
information from those who cannot. By employing a multi-faceted machine learning 
model, our method combines the strengths of diffusion-based models and network 
science to gauge an individual's influence based on their behavior in the 
network. We then employ a series of influence control problems to measure 
user credibility, leveraging the concept of resistance to evaluate their 
credibility. Through our simulations using real-world data from Twitter, we 
demonstrate the superiority of our approach in identifying users with 
established malicious intent and distinguishing them from users with 
established benign intent. This approach yields a high degree of accuracy in 
identifying users with malicious intent, while achieving a high degree of 
precision in distinguishing users with benign intent.

The rapid growth of connected vehicles is driving the development of Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) services and associated smart transportation systems. However, the existing V2X communication model based on direct wireless connections is limited in scale and resource usage. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging the potential of 5G network slicing through Vehicle-to-Everything Network Slice (V2XNS) to support the expansion of Vehicle-to-Everything services. The V2XNS architecture is based on three primary components: virtualized V2X services, a centralized control system, and network slices. By defining the specific attributes for these components, we ensure that V2XNS meets the necessary requirements. Furthermore, we design the V2XNS-fair, V2XNS-safe, and V2XNS-efficient scheduling algorithms to manage and allocate network resources for the network slices. The simulation results demonstrate that V2XNS significantly improves resource efficiency, enhances service quality, and supports the expansion of Vehicle-to-Everything services.

The introduction of robots in manufacturing and healthcare has led to collaborative efforts between humans and robots, with the potential for robots and workers to work alongside each other. To ensure safe interactions, the robot is equipped with safety features that allow it to avoid accidents and prevent harm to human workers. Human-robot collaboration is also beneficial in tasks that require gentle movements, such as handling fragile objects. To achieve this, the robot must communicate effectively with human workers through haptic feedback, also known as human-robot collaboration. Haptic feedback plays a significant role in human-robot collaboration, enabling robots to apply precise forces that promote smooth and efficient interaction. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of haptic feedback in human-robot collaboration, including various control methods and applications. Our analysis reveals key areas for improvement and suggests potential solutions to enhance haptic feedback in human-robot collaboration.

The urban population is projected to increase by 70% overall, and by 1.6% annually from 2015 to 2020. We've compiled a list of the top 100 metropolitan areas from 28 countries, ranking them based on population size. Our primary focus is on Asia, and we note that China, India, and Africa will see the largest growth in urban areas. We've also identified the most rapidly growing cities, both globally and within each country, and selected a specific set of 20 diverse cities for further analysis. This selection is based on factors like the impact of climate change, urban development projects, and the availability of relevant data. We aim to explore the spatial characteristics of these cities, examining the relationships between urban growth, transportation systems, and environmental factors.

In a scenario where users provide items to be cached with probability p and follow a Bernoulli distribution, we investigate a prediction-augmented caching problem to minimize cache miss. A novel algorithm, augmented prediction caching, achieves a competitive ratio of O(1/p) when the overall L1 error is bounded. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of Ω(1/p) for this problem, demonstrating the near-optimality of our proposed algorithm. Additionally, we consider a scenario where the L1 prediction error is within a certain range, finding that our algorithm maintains a competitive ratio of O(log^2 (L/p)) while reducing the L1 regret to O(log^2 (L/p)) times the optimal value.

Accurate segmentation of medical images into distinct anatomical areas is a critical step in medical image analysis, enabling the identification of diseases and quantifying anatomical structures. However, the development of a comprehensive and precise atlas that covers various organs poses a significant challenge due to the complexity and variability of the human body. In this research, we propose a novel approach for constructing a multi-organ atlas by leveraging a pre-trained, unsupervised model and a supervised convolutional neural network. This approach uses the pre-trained model to identify and isolate the regions of interest, which are then input to the supervised network for detailed segmentation. By utilizing the information from the unsupervised model, the supervised network is able to segment the image into organs with high precision, as demonstrated by our experiments using data from 18 patients. In our initial experiment, we successfully built a comprehensive atlas for the abdominal and thoracic organs, including the liver, heart, and lungs, using a small dataset. In our second experiment, we demonstrated that our method can be applied to unseen data from different patients, resulting in a highly accurate multi-organ atlas.

Following Hawking's suggestion to explore the possibility of complete, four-dimensional conformal theories emerging from reduced eleven-dimensional supergravity, we examine the underlying geometry of the reduced theory and show its origin in an eleven-dimensional $G_2$-structure with reduced symmetry, along with a modified view of the reduced theory's field equations. We then derive modified field equations for the reduced four-dimensional theory and propose a solution that corresponds to an evolving de Sitter universe.

Even with the growing focus on data quality, incorrect or misleading instances can still be found in datasets, potentially harming model performance and making it challenging to detect errors. A new method, Contrastive Instance Distancing, has been developed to effectively isolate and remove such problematic instances from training data. This method uses a unique distance metric that calculates instance similarity by comparing feature changes. Contrary to traditional approaches that treat all instances as similar, this new method takes into account the varying levels of feature differences between instances. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that CID is able to detect and isolate instances with significant differences, including those with label discrepancies and noisy data, making it a valuable tool for dataset refinement and enhancing model reliability.

The fundamental concept of the Quantum Hall effect relies on the presence of a
ground state wave function at filling factor $\nu=1$ that remains intact.
This state is modeled by a particular wave function, typically derived from
the so-called Hartree-Fock ground state of a two-dimensional electron gas.
Consequently, the physics of the QHE can be understood by analyzing the wave
function of the lowest Landau level, which is essentially the zero-mode wave function.
This work aims to investigate how the properties of the wave function are affected
by a background potential, using a mean-field approach to solve the problem.
This solution enables us to provide a precise, closed-form expression for the
wave function and its square magnitude, which displays a dip at a particular
point, depending on the position of the minimum of the background potential.
Additionally, we can calculate the dip's depth and width, which are influenced by
the background potential and the strength of the exchange potential, using
analytical expressions.
Notably, the analysis reveals that the dip's depth and width are invariant under
changes in the background potential, which is a fixed property.

Recent advancements in language modeling pretraining have yielded significant
gains in natural language understanding tasks. A key challenge lies in the
requirement for a large-scale, efficiently managed parallelism environment to
process extensive fine-tuning tasks. The proposed METRO training approach aims to
overcome this limitation by dividing language model updates into smaller, more
manageable segments. Through experiments on the M5.4 and mC4 datasets, we
demonstrate that METRO enables the concurrent training of multiple models, which
subsequently achieves comparable performance to the best-existing models.

We investigate the topological characteristics of a quantum network defined by its adjacency matrix. We use quantum information theory to show how measurements of entropies, such as von Neumann entropy and mutual information, can identify the network's adjacency structure. This approach allows us to determine the network's connectivity through its 1- and 2-connected components, which can be further extended to more general graphs. We also outline how the same measurements can be used to identify the network's topological properties.

To effectively convey insights to diverse audiences through visualizations, it is crucial that presenters provide clear explanations and context beforehand. We propose an approach to help designers develop corresponding narratives for their visualizations, ensuring their audience understands the story. Our method involves a structured framework that guides verbal introduction creation by considering the purpose and content of the visual. Through user testing, we discovered that the presenter's introductions significantly impacted viewers interpreting the information presented. The study also reveals how design experts' backgrounds and perspectives influence their ability to create effective narratives for visualizations.

The behavior of highly excited quantum systems is still not well understood, particularly in their equilibrium state. However, in equilibrium, we've found a universal pattern in which many highly excited systems naturally reach a state of maximum entropy when driven continuously. This pattern emerges in a broad class of quantum systems, regardless of how strongly interacting they are. Our findings are most striking in one-dimensional systems with anti-ferromagnetic properties, where the equilibrium state is highly symmetrical and corresponds to a state of maximum entropy. Interestingly, this equilibrium state can be described using a concept called a tensor product structure, which helps to explain the observed entropy. This work provides a framework for understanding the universal properties of highly excited quantum systems, including those in one-dimensional systems with anti-ferromagnetic properties.

Counterfactual explanations are gaining momentum in high-stakes applications like machine learning, social movements, and regulatory compliance.  A counterfactual plan modifies only a limited number of attributes to reverse a true outcome (e.g., a rejected loan) and results in an acceptable true outcome.  To find the best counterfactual plan in terms of attribute changes required, current methods rely on heuristics such as Doppelganger selection or local model optimization.  However, these approaches lack theoretical underpinnings and often result in suboptimal plans due to over-reliance on heuristics.  This paper presents a formal framework for counterfactual plans and develops a mathematical framework called Discrete Counterfactual Search (DCS), which can be applied to various models to find optimal counterfactual plans.  DCS iteratively explores the nearest equivalent instances in the decision boundary through a systematic search approach and has been proven to find a counterfactual plan within a limited number of attribute changes without any restrictions.  Experimental results demonstrate that DCS outperforms current methods in terms of the minimum number of attribute changes required.

Urban sound classification has been gaining significant attention from researchers and policymakers due to its crucial role in monitoring noise pollution, an essential step in enhancing urban quality of life. The growing interest stems from the ability of data-driven approaches to analyze urban soundscapes, identify stressors like traffic noise, and inform noise reduction strategies. Our study contributes a novel contribution by introducing a comprehensive dataset of 7,982 audio clips annotated with traffic sounds (or not) and categorizing them into four distinct urban sound elements (car, engine, horn, or none). The dataset, named UTS-TCDD, is designed to address the need for large-scale datasets in the field, enabling machine learning model development for traffic sound classification. We evaluate the performance of various machine learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines and Convolutional Neural Networks, and find that deep learning networks, particularly the CNN with a MobileNet backbone, yield the best results. The proposed dataset is available at the link https://github.com/irinewk/UTS-TCDD.

We investigate the properties of supersymmetric solutions in N=3 gauged supergravity with the SO(3) x SO(3) and SO(3) symmetries by solving the BPS equations. The equations are solved exactly for the case with SO(3) x SO(3) symmetry and numerically for the case with SO(3) symmetry. The existence of supersymmetric AdS_4 vacua is confirmed for both cases. The BPS solutions with SO(3) x SO(3) symmetry have finite energy and are stable. The BPS solutions with SO(3) symmetry have infinite energy but are also stable. The study of these solutions reveals a connection between N=3 gauged supergravity and Einstein-Maxwell gravity with a double scalar field. The study also shows that the SO(3) x SO(3) vacua are connected to the AdS_4 vacuum with a specific value for the gauge coupling and the scalar field. The study also reveals a connection between N=3 gauged supergravity and SO(2) gauged supergravity. The study provides evidence for the equivalence between N=3 gauged supergravity and Einstein-Maxwell gravity with a double scalar field. The study also provides evidence for the connection between N=3 gauged supergravity and SO(2) gauged supergravity.

The increasing demand for edge computing is driving the need for innovative architectures, with a growing emphasis on hardware-based acceleration. One promising approach is the integration of image signal processing into sensor processors, allowing for real-time computation in the sensor itself. This concept of Focal-plane Sensor-processors, or FPSPs, has the potential to minimize data transmission and enable low-power, high-throughput inference. However, the successful implementation of these processors requires a thorough understanding of their suitability for diverse machine learning tasks. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating the limitations of sensor-based processing for various CNN workloads. We developed the HEDGES framework, which evaluates the performance of different processors and considers their inherent strengths and weaknesses. Our results demonstrate that, while current CPUs perform better in certain tasks, the processing capabilities within integrated graphics chips are more comparable to those of specialized CPUs. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the potential for improvement in these architectures through architectural modifications and more efficient communication methods.

Generalized $\theta$-terms, which are a key component of global symmetries in effective field theories, are being utilized to explain the absence of (e/e)5 physics in type IIB string theory on a Calabi-Yau manifold with a flux. We have identified a 2d Hamiltonian from the 2d Hamiltonian reduction of 6d hypermultiplet Lagrangism, incorporating a specific set of generalized $\theta$-terms, which are a higher-dimensional analog of Wess-Zumino terms. These terms are a natural extension of previously studied topological terms, specifically the Chern-Simons and Pfaffian terms found in 3d topological insulators/superconductors. A novel, exactly solvable Hamiltonian was derived, which is a solvable model of the (2,0) theory, and its 4d Lagrangian form was reconstructed. This reconstruction resulted in a set of known terms, including Pfaffian terms, which are a summand of the topological Lagrangian, and novel terms that are a contribution to the generalized $\theta$-angles. These novel terms were found to be a consequence of a 2d version of a 4d phenomenon, the anomaly cancellation of gauge/gravity $\theta$-angles.

In empirical game-theoretic analysis, the behavior of a game is approximated by collecting data from interactions between the system and its environment.  Utilizing an oracle, which can simulate the behavior of the system, can enhance the accuracy of game-theoretic analysis by incorporating real-world data into the model.  This research presents a method to integrate an oracle's data into model-based game-theoretic analysis, specifically for games characterized by a finite number of states, actions, and non-biased, noise-free oracle responses.  The developed technique, ORCA, combines the data collected from oracle responses and system queries through a weighted average, adjusting the weights according to a specific loss function.  By iteratively updating these weights, ORCA aims to minimize the loss function, ultimately yielding more accurate system behavior estimates.  The research also provides theoretical support for ORCA, specifically for its application with Blackwell-type and regret minimization algorithms, demonstrating that it can produce consistent estimates as data is collected.  The effectiveness of ORCA is further validated through its application to two empirical examples.

We suggest a novel modal logic with a restricted epistemic and an endogenous probability framework that integrates the spirit of Aristotle's modal syllogistic theory. This logic enables us to define and establish the validity of the modal syllogisms that Aristotle considered pivotal, thereby fulfilling the key objective of our proposed modal system.

Quantum causality is a fundamental aspect of quantum theory, and it can be tested by measuring correlations between quantum systems. Researchers have developed a method called causal inequalities, which can detect causal quantum effects. To observe this effect, it is crucial to have a high detection efficiency of at least 50%. To improve this, a new method of causal inequality is proposed, called the generalized causal inequality, which only requires a minimum of 1% detection efficiency to observe quantum causality. This inequality investigates relationships between outcomes of measurements on a tripartite quantum system. The study further found that all causal classical inequalities fail at 50% detection efficiency and fail to match their quantum counterparts at 1% detection efficiency.

This research introduces an innovative prediction method based on spatial and temporal features for frame-level bit allocation in the HEVC/H.265 video codec standard. The objective is to optimize quality through the allocation of available bits to individual video frames while maintaining conformity to rate control parameters. A proposed solution employs a neural network with two distinct networks: a regression network for estimating frame quality, and a classification network for identifying suitable quantization levels. These networks were pre-trained using a unique label assignment method that maps ground-truth quality metrics to rate levels, then fine-tuned to optimize prediction accuracy. The neural networks were found to significantly enhance prediction precision and performance, achieving significant reductions in bitmasks and bitrate errors compared to the original HEVC/H.265 rate control.

The abundance of C2H in the gas phase is a key factor in understanding the chemical composition of protoplanetary disks, but the C/O ratio has a significant impact on its abundance. Studies of C2H in the gas phase and solids have shown a higher abundance in disks with high C/O ratios, but the reason behind this discrepancy remains unclear. This study investigates the origin of C2H in disks with high C/O ratios by examining the interaction between C2H and C2H2, and C2H2 and C2H. Results show that the reaction of C2H with C2H2 is the primary source of C2H in disks with high C/O ratios. This reaction is more efficient than other processes, and it can explain why C2H is more abundant in disks with high C/O ratios. Additionally, our study suggests that the C2H/C2H2 ratio may be used to determine the C/O ratio in disks with abundant C2H, which could provide insights into the disk formation processes.

Cutting planes play a vital role in solving mixed-integer linear problems. To enhance cutting plane selection, we propose a novel approach that combines a graph neural network with state-of-the-art solving methods. By converting a branched solution space into a static graph, our model learns to identify branch-and-bound search targets using cut effectiveness as its target. Through a unique, problem-specific training process, the model becomes proficient in predicting the effectiveness of various cutting planes. Initial results demonstrate that our solution to MILP problems, when combined with a state-of-the-art solving method, outperforms current benchmarks across different studies and benchmark problems.

A specific type of material, calcium niobate, has been found to exhibit unique topological properties when doped with iridium. The unique quantum Hall effect observed under a strong magnetic field, like a 14.1 Tesla field, is consistent with theoretical models. However, the application of a lower-strength magnetic field, below 2 Tesla, reveals a distinct pattern of shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in the electrical conductivity of the material. The analysis of these oscillations, using a light-based technique, has allowed researchers to determine the 3D electron dispersion. The data shows that the material exhibits a complex structure, consisting of two sets of electron pockets with different properties, and further research is needed to understand the origin of this phenomenon.

Duplicate bug report detection is a significant issue in large-scale bug tracking systems. Identifying and consolidating such reports not only saves developers time but also improves bug diagnosis and analysis. However, existing solutions, which rely on various features, are often hindered by feature extraction inefficiencies and require substantial human oversight. In response, we propose a novel approach, Cross-Model Feature Selection, which utilizes a combination of multiple feature types and creates a dynamic, cross-model search space for selecting optimal features. Our approach also incorporates a unique feature filtering mechanism, eliminating the need for excessive feature calculations and reducing the search space. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art techniques, while significantly reducing computational costs.

Our research focuses on the impact of anisotropy on phase transitions governed by essential kinetic constraints. The anisotropy influences the system's behavior, altering critical coupling values and resulting observables. We derive an analytical formula for the anisotropic round-trip group average and connect it to the round-trip method of the renormalization group flow. This connection enables us to determine the critical coupling using the multicomponent cubic anisotropic scalar field theory. The analytical results are consistent with previous findings from numerical simulations.

Traditional supervised learning approaches for Named Entity Recognition (NER) rely heavily on extensive labeled datasets. However, this requirement for large datasets restricts the application of NER in scenarios where labelled data is scarce, a common occurrence. To address this limitation, a new framework has been developed for Distantly-Supervised NER (DS-NER) that leverages large amounts of unlabelled texts. This framework enables DS-NER with the use of a semi-supervised model that incorporates both labelled and unlabelled data during training. Furthermore, an adaptable pseudo label correction mechanism has been implemented to refine the accuracy of generated pseudo labels. Consequently, this approach enhances the performance of DS-NER by utilizing the pseudo labels. To further assess its effectiveness, this framework was tested on multiple NER datasets and compared against established DS-NER methods. As a result, it achieved superior results, demonstrating 7.5% and 5.5% higher F1 scores for NER on Clusters and WikiCS datasets respectively.

As digital data and social networks grow, understanding the sentiment and opinions expressed by individuals within them becomes increasingly vital. Tracking these online conversations helps businesses to identify and analyze patterns of consumer feedback and sentiment on the internet, particularly on platforms like Twitter where users frequently share their experiences and views about various products and services. This research aims to explore the use of machine learning techniques for sentiment analysis on Twitter data. The analysis utilizes an assortment of text features and incorporates different search queries to identify relevant tweets relevant to specific products such as Apple iPhone and Samsung Galaxy. The extracted text features are then utilized to train support vector machine (SVM) and naive bayes classifiers to determine the sentiment expressed in each tweet. Furthermore, the incorporation of bag-of-words, n-gram features, and part-of-speech features allows for classification of the sentiment of each tweet. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in accurately classifying the sentiment of tweets, achieving an accuracy rate of 80%.

A detailed analysis of the effective heat conductivity of highly heterogeneous microstructured materials is performed using a two-temperature approach in the linearly deformable material model framework. The influence of various material parameters on the effective conductivity is studied through a series of material parameter combinations. The findings are substantiated by numerical solutions to the heat equation and compared with existing experimental data. The study reveals that the material parameter combinations have a profound effect on the effective heat conductivity. The outcomes provide valuable insights for designing microstructured materials with tailored thermal properties to meet specific application requirements. This research ultimately contributes to the development of novel, advanced materials with tailored thermal properties that can be utilized in next-generation thermal energy converters.

The exoplanet CI Tau b, a massive Jupiter mass planet, orbits the $\beta$ Pne-like star CI Tau within 4 days, and its unique characteristics hint at a complex formation process. By employing high-resolution optical spectroscopy via the CARMENES database, researchers have observed the star's radial velocity variations and its host star's physical properties. They discovered that the planet's eccentricity is likely to be high, and its orbital period is 4.5 days, which may suggest an extraordinary migration history. Furthermore, the star's infrared radiation indicates the presence of a pre-main-sequence disk with a mass of at least 0.05 solar masses, and its age is estimated to be 2-5 million years.

In Newtonian mechanics, the orbit of a particle is determined by its initial conditions and position on the orbit, with the force exerted on the particle being a function of its position and the properties of the force field. A novel approach presented in this study enables the derivation of an expression for the force in terms of the orbit's parameters, eliminating the need to account for the force's specific central or non-central nature. This expression can be obtained by considering a specific set of reference curves, with the derivation process being illustrated using a non-central force field and a circular curve. With the results obtained, we address the paradox of a self-intersecting curve not altering the force experienced by the points of intersection, with the effects of this self-intersection on the force being represented by the curvature of the curve and the force's properties. Finally, the study provides a general expression for the force in the context of a rotating reference frame.

This article establishes the fractional Sobolev space on compact complete connected Riemannian manifolds, proving the existence of the fractional Sobolev quotient and identifying its optimal constant. We demonstrate that this optimal constant is equivalent to the infimum of the Poincaré ratio constants of all K isometrically convex compact Riemannian manifolds.

This research focuses on multi-object filtering and presents a novel approach using sequential Monte Carlo within a graph network framework. The method employs a multi-trajectory particle smoother to estimate the joint state of all objects and a graph neural network to compute object-level features from trajectories. The graph network's initial weights are set to zero, and the final state is passed through the network to compute object associations at each time step. The performance of the network heavily relies on its ability to identify and correct association errors, making it crucial to incorporate this in the learning objective. The proposed method was evaluated on a public benchmark, demonstrating competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer particles.

The growing number of power electronics converters and poorly damped AC systems is giving rise to concerns about interactions between them and the grid. In particular, researchers are investigating transient interactions between large-scale grid-scale PV systems and nearby power systems. This study examines the effects of a large-scale grid-scale PV system on a small-scale power system when the latter experiences a disturbance. To analyze these effects, a new method is presented that combines frequency-domain analysis and linear models to predict transient dynamics. This approach is applied to a real-world case study involving a 105 MW grid-scale PV system and a 60 MW power system, demonstrating its practical utility.

This research introduces three metrics to effectively capture and represent online signature templates, including the Signature Segmentation Metric, which segments the signature into different zones and calculates the average distance of a signature in each zone, the Signature Repeating Pattern Metric, which counts repeated signature patterns, and the Signature Salient Zone Extraction Metric, which extracts significant areas of a signature and calculates their total distance. We then compared the performance of these metrics with the standard online signature verification features provided by the KASVS-ESIGN dataset, and evaluated their ability to distinguish between genuine and forgery signatures.

This paper presents a novel method to count the number of lattice points within any triangle whose vertex coordinates are rational. This approach draws on two key elements: employing Euclidean approximations of the triangle's vertex coordinates, obtained from the continued fraction expansion; and leveraging the concept of the Hilbert lattice, a lattice within the plane defined by rational vector combinations. Classically, the count for triangles with integer vertex coordinates is determined by Pick's formula. Extending this principle, we develop a "rational Pick formula" applicable to any triangle with vertex coordinates featuring rational numbers.

Modern mobile applications often have to accommodate a wide range of features, 
which can be very resource-intensive, yet still benefit a substantial portion of users.
This problem can be addressed by an innovative approach called context-oriented 
programming that enables different system components to be used only when specific user contexts dictate it.
However, this context-oriented approach necessitates the development of separate components for each scenario.
We propose an alternative solution, called partial orienting, which optimizes performance in context-sensitive scenarios by only considering relevant contexts at the time of need.
We have developed a tool that integrates partial orienting with a language like Lisp and evaluated its effectiveness using real-world examples.

This paper introduces an innovative attention mechanism designed to enhance pose estimation for challenging cases. Conventional pose estimation methods rely on standard back-propagation to fine-tune model parameters, but this approach often falls short due to suboptimal initial keypoint positions. To address this limitation, our proposed attention mechanism focuses on identifying and highlighting key discriminative regions within images. By introducing a receptive field to highlight image areas of high discriminative value, we can concentrate training efforts on these regions and improve pose estimation accuracy. To facilitate this process, we have developed a training strategy that involves the simultaneous training of keypoint refinement networks with reduced keypoints. This approach allows us to refine the performance of our model when keypoints are abundant, while resampling and attention mechanisms enable optimal performance when keypoints are scarce. Our proposed method has been thoroughly evaluated and validated through extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets: Human3.6M, 2D-Multiveiw, and Natural Language Descriptions. The results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in improving pose estimation, particularly in challenging cases.

A technique for measuring the intensity of celestial sources is developed by analyzing how their observed counts change when they get hidden by the Earth. This method uses data collected over a long time period, such as those from monitoring systems, and uses an autoregressive model to find the source intensities. This method's accuracy is tested by comparing it to a standard method that doesn't take into account the time series data. It's demonstrated that this method can accurately detect occultations and use them to calculate the source intensities. This method is then applied to the most energetic gamma-ray sources, such as the blazar 3C 279, and finds that their fluxes change significantly on a time scale of days. It's also observed that this method's fluxes have a good correlation with those from the Fermi Large Area Telescope, with a good sensitivity and accuracy for detecting occultations of less than 3 minutes.

While the theoretical soundness of consensus protocols is well-understood, real-world performance remains a subject of debate, with the industry and academia differing in their assessment. This paper delves into the comparison of various blockchain protocols with a focus on protocol-specific properties such as latency, finality, and conservation of energy. To facilitate this analysis, we establish a framework for characterizing these properties based on the impact they have when put to practical test. We then use this framework to evaluate the behavior of different blockchain protocols, including energy consumption, by running experiments on multiple networks. The results of our study, which to our knowledge represents the first of its kind for PoW and PoS networks, are compared and contrasted to reveal key similarities and differences between the two.

The tetraquark states with two heavy quarks are prime candidates for exotic states and can be effectively studied using the Fierz-Sala model with constituent quarks. In this model, the inter-quark potential is a combination of a linearly rising confining potential and a Coulomb potential. This paper explores the mass spectra of such tetraquark states comprising a combination of heavy and light quarks, specifically considering the S-wave and P-wave configurations. A notable feature of these tetraquark states is their parity inversion relative to mesons, resulting in the absence of a linear Regge trajectory. Instead, the energy of these tetraquark states increases in a parabolic manner with angular momentum.

We've developed a new approach to assess the metastability of the electroweak vacuum that's based on the effective potential of a theoretical model. This approach centers on the minimum of the potential's global minimum, which is a parameter-agnostic value, and the scale at which the theory loses its validity. By considering the running Higgs mass within this approach, specifically how it changes as the scale changes, we've found that this metastability is tied to the rate at which the Higgs mass changes. This method is applicable to a wide range of theories and model types, and it doesn't rely on any specific assumptions about their parameters or behavior. We've successfully demonstrated this approach using the two-Higgs-doublet model, and the results show that the method is consistent with existing knowledge from this model.

We prove the $q-$Logarithmic Sobolev inequality for probability measures defined in terms of Carnot-Carathéodory distance in Carnot groups. Additionally, we establish the free Carnot group version of the free ln-Sobolev inequality. The proof relies on establishing a discrete version of the ln-Sobolev inequality for free and uniform continuous density functions with specific properties.

This research develops a broad family of estimators, the total variance estimator, designed to minimize Bregman divergences in a wide range of parameter spaces. We establish that this total variance estimator is a unique M-estimator for any parameter of interest and that it can be considered an extension of the DPD class of estimators. Notably, the total variance estimator is shown to be an adaptive procedure in a broad context. Additionally, the total variance estimator is found to perform well under conditions of high bias and large data sizes. We also conduct a comparative analysis of the total variance estimator and the DPD class of estimators in a range of simulated scenarios and real-world datasets, finding that the total variance estimator generally outperforms the DPD class of estimators in our simulations, and its performance aligns well with the DPD class in our analyses of real-world datasets.

We propose a novel approach, based on a self-supervised neural radiance model, designed to generate a 6K resolution virtual view of a dynamic unstructured scene from a single source video in real-time. Our method, built on a hierarchical neural radiance field, has been enhanced with a dynamic rendering technique that utilizes a spatial-temporal neural network. This network is trained end-to-end using a self-supervised learning framework that utilizes a large collection of YouTube videos to predict future scenes from a given source video. Our experiments demonstrate superior results over existing methods in dynamic scene synthesis and show promising potential for future applications.

We study the statistics of chaotic quantum graphs consisting of a specific configuration with three connected interlocking cylinders, each representing a quantum graph that is topologically equivalent to an infinite line. The graph features a single vertex where three lines intersect and where four different infinite lines merge into a single line, all containing a potential with two separate energy levels. Two of these cylinders are identical, while the third has a unique potential shape that can either match the others or be different. We have determined the lengths of specific stable trajectories within this configuration and have calculated the lengths of specific stable and unstable paths by using a previously developed method.
