This research will enable us to pinpoint areas where these services fail to meet accessibility criteria and provide data-driven solutions to rectify these shortcomings.

The challenge of the one-shot continual learning task in machine learning has been overcome by employing a generative model to generate training images from a limited set of learned examples, however this approach still has its drawbacks. In an effort to improve the efficacy of the model, we've developed a new one-shot learning technique that incorporates the principles of few-shot continual learning and uses a strategy to minimize the memory usage by continually updating the model with new concepts while discarding the least important information. In order to minimize the negative effects of this process, we've developed an approach to monitor the learning process and prevent the model from forgetting previously learned information. Experimental results have shown that our proposed technique is effective, even when there is limited data available.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning heavily relies on the quality of its training dataset.  However, the presence of biases in these datasets poses a significant risk, leading to unfair and potentially hazardous outcomes in real-world applications.  To address this concern, we developed a novel dataset augmentation method that involves modifying the Dicom header of images to counteract biases.  Our experiments on multiple large-scale datasets revealed that the proposed approach yields substantial improvements in performance, with consistent boosts in accuracy observed across datasets.  Our research demonstrates the efficacy of this method in minimizing data biases and promoting more equitable and accurate AI-driven medical image analysis.

Deep Metric Learning systems have achieved notable success in various computer vision tasks. However, they are easily compromised by noisy labels since the noisy labels distort the distance between samples and the model's representation. Existing approaches to addressing label noise in ML systems typically involve data cleaning methods that remove noisy data or modify learning objectives to reduce the impact of noise. We propose an innovative approach to address label noise in ML systems. We develop a method to create a noise-free training set by identifying and eliminating noisy labels in a training dataset. We achieve this by leveraging the model's ability to generate new representations that conform to its understanding of a class by manipulating a clean training point within its class boundary. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using several ML systems and a variety of datasets, and our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

A widely used tool for analyzing the distribution of matter in the universe, known as the 2-point statistics, can be expanded to a more advanced statistical measure known as the 3-point statistics or three-point function. This more complex analysis method is used to measure the clustering of the universe and can be applied to a survey known as the Dark Energy Survey. We have developed a new way to analyze the distribution of galaxies in DES Year 3 by using a measure that represents the distribution of the universe, known as the N-point function. This analysis method is used to measure the distribution of galaxies in survey regions with varying levels of detail. We have also developed a new way to analyze the distribution of galaxies in survey regions with specific properties. This more complex analysis method is used to measure the distribution of galaxies in the survey regions with specific properties. We have also developed a new way to analyze the distribution of galaxies in the survey regions with specific properties. This is a preliminary study to measure the distribution of galaxies in the survey regions with specific properties.

Recent discoveries of superfluid $^3$He have motivated researchers to develop a new, topological superfluid that can also exhibit unusual, "topological" properties. This paper outlines the theoretical development of an advanced, topological superfluid that can be achieved in a $^3$He system. This "topological" superfluid arises from a combination of three distinct components: (i) a standard superfluid with an $SO(5)$ symmetry, (ii) a topological $^3$He superconductor with an $SO(5)$ symmetry, and (iii) a topological $^3$He superconductor with an $SO(5)$ symmetry and zero residual density. This unique combination of properties enables the emergence of topological features such as gapless, Dirac excitations, and a fourfold quantum phase diagram. This topological superfluid can be achieved using a $^3$He-$^3$H two-dimensional lattice with an $SO(5)$ symmetry and can be controlled by tuning the $^3$He superconductor's gap and the $^3$He-$^3$H hopping amplitude. This new, topological superfluid opens the possibility of observing and studying topological features in superconductors.

Recent advancements in micropixel avalanche photodiodes have led to significant improvements in scintillation detectors, primarily due to their exceptional sensitivity and low-noise capabilities. This study introduces a novel approach by integrating a micropixel avalanche photodiode with a silicon photomultiplier to create a fast and efficient light sensor. The silicon photomultiplier serves as an amplifier for the micropixel avalanche photodiode, and the combination is successfully demonstrated through various tests, including the measurement of the coincidence time and energy resolution of the $^{22}$Na source. The results demonstrate a coincidence time of less than 600 picoseconds and an energy resolution of approximately 8.3 percent.

This note offers an alternative proof of the Cohen-Macaulay local ring definition using
valuations and their primary ideals, thereby linking Salzer's concept of valuations to
Cohen-Macaulay rings to reduce dimension growth in a polynomial ring.

Our research involves the study of underdoped Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high-pressure conditions, specifically its structural, electrical, and magnetic characteristics.  Through x-ray diffraction analysis, we found that the pressure-induced expansion along the c-axis is significantly greater than the expansion in the a/b plane.  As pressure increased, the material's lattice dimensions in the a/b plane decreased, while the c-axis lattice dimension increased.  By combining x-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction techniques, we found that the material's magnetic ordering is suppressed at low temperatures, specifically, below 50 K.  Furthermore, we discovered that the material's magnetic ordering is suppressed in a first-order manner.  As pressure increased, the material's Curie temperature also increased, specifically, by 20 K at 7 GPa.  Our findings indicate that the material's magnetic ordering is highly sensitive to external pressure, specifically, that the material becomes magnetically disordered under relatively low pressure conditions.

This paper develops a Bayesian framework for assessing joint statistical significance by accounting for the high incidence of zero and long-tailed values in various financial benchmarks. It also showcases how our approach can successfully extract multiple significant factors influencing stock prices while mitigating the issue of false discoveries. Furthermore, a comprehensive simulation study confirms the efficacy of our methodology in accurately detecting joint statistical significance across diverse parameterization scenarios.

A double-disk cavity optomechanical system has been found to be highly manipulable within the Lamb shift range. By using two closely positioned disks in an optomechanical cavity and adjusting their distance, we can fine-tune the system's resonant frequencies and achieve a broad spectrum of a single low-order optical mode with minimal losses. The created system exhibits exceptional performance as a tunable optical filter, capable of handling high volumes of data and demonstrating low power losses during transmission. Through simulations, we found that this system can filter out side modes by more than 30 dB, resulting in a maximum drop efficiency of 97.5% within the optomechanical range. Furthermore, we investigated how the system's performance is affected by various system parameters, such as disk distance, optical mode number, and optical power, allowing for a better understanding of its capabilities.

Public health interventions serve as key drivers of progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals outlined by the World Health Organization.  The WHO Global Health Estimates provide a framework for tracking global progress but have limitations in terms of timeliness and granularity.  Online interaction offers a window into individual lives, reflecting the impact of interventions on daily behavior.  This work presents a method for leveraging online data to gauge the effectiveness of interventions.  The proposed approach employs a multi-step process of isolating information related to interventions and aggregating data at the national level.  The technique is demonstrated using Twitter data and public health information from 33 countries, highlighting the potential for improving the speed and detail of assessment while reducing costs.

In several image processing tasks like video conferencing and data storage, achieving high compression ratios at fast compression rates is crucial. Current video coding standards reach peak quality at compression levels of 60:1, but only reach half of that quality at the necessary rates of 120:1, and thus there's room for improvement. A new approach called SpeedOptimUS was created to bridge this gap. It involves a two-stage compression process: the first stage uses a detailed encoder to find the best possible compression, and then the second stage uses an efficient encoder to apply that compression without sacrificing too much quality. The key innovation here is that the first stage uses detailed encoding to determine the best possible compression, and then uses that information to speed up the second stage without needing to re-do the detailed encoding. This results in a significant 1.56 dB quality improvement at the necessary rates of 120:1 while only slowing down the compression process by about 10%.

The $B^{+} \to D^{+}_{S} K^{+} K^{-}$ decay process is explored using $1.0$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from the $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$ pair production reaction in $pp$ collisions at a $7$ TeV center-of-mass energy. The data collected by the Belle experiment in 2011 is utilized, with a signal-to-background ratio of approximately $12$ out of $100$. The branching fraction for this decay is calculated to be $(8.5 \pm 2.5 \pm 2.0) \times 10^{-5}$, with the first error representing statistical uncertainty and the second for systematic uncertainty. The discovery of $B^{+} \to D^{+}_{S} K^{+} K^{-}$ is the first reported instance of $\bar{B}^{0}_{s} \to D^{+}_{S} K^{+} K^{-}$ decay, with a branching fraction for $\bar{B}^{0}_{S} \to D^{+}_{S} K^{+} K^{-}$ calculated as $(4.5 \pm 2.5 \pm 1.5) \times 10^{-4}$.

Optimal transport distance has gained significant traction in machine learning, partly due to its robustness to outliers. However, when using outlier-robust loss functions involving optimal transport, the situation is more complex. In a related project, the author and colleagues developed a robust optimization algorithm for Huber loss functions. Here, the problem of optimizing semidefinite programming (SDP) related to optimal transport is tackled, with Huber distance serving as a loss function. By applying the methods from the previous project, the proposed method is able to handle both outlying data points and anomalous optimization data. Experiments confirm that the proposed method outperforms alternative approaches, such as removing outliers or using robust optimization, in the context of semisupervised clustering.

The traditional AI research approach, which typically pits a machine learning model against a human player, has limitations when it comes to real-world applications. The challenge becomes more complex when AI agents must collaborate with humans to achieve optimal outcomes. This paper addresses this issue by developing a human-AI collaboration task based on the popular strategic card game Hanabi. The game poses significant challenges to AI agents due to the need for self-supervised learning and the ability to reason about the human player's actions. Our proposed model successfully adapts to new strategies, which are learned through self-play and self-exploration. The model also demonstrates robust performance in human-AI collaborations by effectively predicting the human's actions and improving overall results.

The investigation of the Higgs boson's mass has been a core aspect of quantum field theory since its inception. This article provides an overview of the current state of research on Higgs boson physics within a supergravity framework. Specifically, we examine how the Higgs boson's mass is calculated using a combination of the effective potential and the $\epsilon$-expansion method, which we believe will help us accurately predict the mass up to four-loop order and potentially beyond. Our long-term goal is to provide a precise, quantitative understanding of the Higgs boson's properties, which we hope will be achieved by integrating our research with other cutting-edge projects in supersymmetry and the Green's function approach.

Our study involves a multi-disciplinary group of individuals with varying levels of cognitive abilities and professional backgrounds who were asked to use and interact with a complex spatial visualization tool on a 360-degree panoramic image of a building over a virtual tour map. Our findings reveal significant differences in how users navigate and utilize the visualization, showing that spatial abilities significantly impact an individual's ability to do so, particularly when faced with unfamiliar navigation tasks. Our results suggest that traditional navigation methods may hinder some individuals' ability to access information, and we identify potential design issues for the visualization tool, recommending strategies to enhance its usability and accessibility. Our study underscores the importance of considering users' spatial abilities in the design process and provides new insights for improving spatial visualization capabilities.

This paper explores the application of automated theorem proving to cycle elimination within first-order automated theorem proving, a task previously considered complicated due to the NP-hard cycle detection problem. We propose a method to validate the soundness of a cycle elimination procedure, which is based on a new, compact clause format. The procedure is derived from an automated induction process for the universal 1 arithmetic formula, yielding a straightforward proof. We also demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on a set of testing models.

Recent advancements in neural network-based graph retrieval methods have led to the development of innovative techniques such as GNNIR and SGNN. These methods, however, are hindered by their inability to handle large-scale information networks and high-speed data streams in real-time settings. To address this limitation, a novel approach is proposed by combining GNNIR with streaming data buffers to efficiently process queries and retrieve relevant results promptly.

Recent advancements in machine learning and data-driven techniques have led to breakthroughs in computer vision and natural language processing. The fields of computer vision and natural language processing have shown significant overlap in their goals and applications, and this paper reviews the increasing number of shared projects and techniques. The review begins by identifying key applications and processes in computer vision and natural language processing, highlighting areas where these fields are converging and intersecting. The convergence of computer vision and natural language processing has resulted in the emergence of new fields, such as image captioning and visual question-ansering, which are shaped by the increasing availability of large image datasets and machine learning algorithms. The review explores the role of deep learning in natural language processing and computer vision, discusses the application of text analysis techniques to enhance image recognition, and examines the use of natural language processing methods for image segmentation. The convergence of computer vision and natural language processing has led to the development of techniques such as image-text matching, visual text recognition, and image captioning. The review also discusses the challenges faced in integrating the two fields and provides insights into future directions and applications.

In countries with rapidly evolving economies, electricity demand significantly increases, often exceeding that of the power grid's capacity. This discrepancy results in widespread and unpredictable power outages, particularly affecting households with substantial electricity needs. Moreover, existing research primarily focuses on the financial impact of power outages on households rather than their daily lives. This study conducts a comprehensive survey of households in Pakistan, which has struggled with a chronic power crisis, to comprehensively assess the impact of power outages on their lives. Our findings indicate that households in resource-constrained regions are disproportionately affected by power outages, and the impact extends beyond economic losses to include more significant daily life disruptions. We further explore how the duration and frequency of power outages influence household productivity and stress levels, ultimately demonstrating the profound effects of load shedding on the lives of individuals in developing countries. Our research findings are intended to inform policy decisions aimed at mitigating the social effects of power outages.

A fundamental task in event research is identifying event occurrences (decks) in documents. However, a common challenge in existing approaches is a critical problem that arises when multiple event occurrences coexist in the same document. To address this, we introduce a new problem where the goal is to automatically determine the number of event occurrences (decks) in a document. To tackle this, we have developed a solution based on a neural network model that predicts both the number of decks and their corresponding positions. By achieving this, we have laid the groundwork for future advancements that incorporate this information to enhance event detection. Our proposed model outperformed existing state-of-the-art models in experiments involving two different types of event data.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem, a more complex variant of the traditional knapsack problem, involves items with conflicting attributes that require careful balancing, given a limited capacity set. This challenging problem has garnered significant attention in the operations research field, where various heuristic methods have been employed to find approximate solutions. However, little research has focused on using machine learning algorithms to tackle CKP. This study bridges that gap, introducing a machine learning approach that combines Bayesian Optimization and Gaussian Processes to yield high-quality solutions. Through comparative analysis with established iterative methods on diverse CKP instances, the findings indicate that machine learning-based heuristics exhibit superior performance in many cases, making them viable alternatives to current methods.

This paper defines and examines generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations and generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivable maps within the context of a semiprime ring, detailing certain characteristics of a generalized $(m,n)$-derivation and offering conditions under which a quotient ring remains generalised $(m,n)$-derivable. Additionally, it provides specific conditions under which a commutative semiprime ring fulfills the generalized $(m,n)$-derivation criterion.

In our research, we investigate a comprehensive set of five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein gravitons in a space with a specific type of metric, involving a dilaton field. By developing an algorithmic approach, we identify the all-order solutions to a system of linear equations and derive the general forms of both the bosonic tree and one-loop Feynman diagrams. The research further extends to the study of a specific class of string theories, where we analyze the low-energy behavior by considering the universal limits of both the bosonic tree and one-loop amplitudes. The constructed amplitude exhibits a factorized structure, with a specific form that includes a universal function related to the Kaluza-Klein tower. The derived amplitude is consistent with the known results at the leading order and demonstrates the emergence of a specific form at the subleading order.

To understand the structure of a set in higher dimensions, we use a method that combines geometry and analysis. This approach is based on a nonlinear concept called Favard length. Our research focuses on the short-term decay rates of an advanced version of Favard length, specifically under nonlinear conditions. By linking Favard length to a concept called thermality, we discover an exact relationship. This relationship helps us determine the decay rates by analyzing the properties of a special function. If the dimension is 2 or higher, we find that these decay rates are influenced by the lowest possible eigenvalue of a specific operator. This operator is related to the Laplacian and measures how much a function deviates from being thermally neutral. If the dimension is 1, we use a method that combines geometry and analysis to precisely describe the decay rates of Favard length. This approach involves understanding how the thermality of a function changes and using a special tool to precisely describe its properties.

A computationally efficient variant of Model Predictive Control with robust outcomes is proposed. This variant, referred to as Robust Tube Control, utilizes a forward-computed, parameter-uncertain, time-varying tube centered on a base policy optimized for the nominal system. Nonlinear programming is used in the cost function to minimize maximum expected deviation from the tube. For linear systems, this problem is computationally intractable due to nested conic programming. A solution to this issue is provided by approximating the tube using linear state transition matrices. Using this approximation, a method for calculating robust outcomes in linear systems is presented along with a simplified approach to improve computational efficiency. Additionally, this paper shows that robust tube control can be extended to nonlinear systems under certain conditions of Lipschitz continuity.

In a specific type of topological material, a unique effect occurs when magnetic fields are applied. This phenomenon is attributed to a specific property called Berry curvature, which exhibits certain characteristics. While typically Berry curvature depends on magnetic fields, a related property called geometric Berry curvature can also be influenced by other types of driving forces. In this research, we have discovered a distinct form of geometric Berry curvature that is tied to the band structure of materials. By studying a specific model of a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal, we have identified this new curvature and its effects on an unusual Hall phenomenon. Notably, we have found that this effect can be controlled by specific symmetry properties and that it leads to an unusual pattern of conductivity that changes direction under certain conditions. Our findings provide new insights into how magnetic fields can induce novel transport effects in materials, which can facilitate the discovery of topological materials with unique properties.

Visualizing the computational structure of large-scale parallel programs is a complex task. Our study focuses on developing methods for displaying the computational structure of multi-threaded programs efficiently. To this end, we created the ensemble-Sankey, a modified Sankey-Sankey diagram that displays call graph data through Sankey tubes. Our proposed approach uses a call graph to identify the computational flow between different parallel components and showcases the data distribution along the Sankey tubes. Our method was applied to a real-world scenario using a large-scale program with multiple threads, and the results show that the ensemble-Sankey effectively captures the computational structure of the program across different thread configurations. The proposed approach offers a range of benefits, including ease of comprehension, reduced complexity, and the ability to quickly and accurately analyze large-scale call graphs.

The performance of highly advanced language models, such as BERT and XLNet, has been impressive in various tasks and applications. However, these models often struggle with adapting to changing datasets, like news articles that update frequently. One such challenge is keeping up with shifting language patterns and terminology that emerge over time. To mitigate this issue, data augmentation techniques can be applied to the original dataset to create an evolving training dataset. In this study, we examine the impact of incorporating news article summaries as auxiliary data to enhance the performance of language models, specifically BERT, in predicting news article titles. Our results demonstrate that leveraging news article summaries as additional training data can indeed improve BERT's ability to generate accurate news article headings.

This review summarizes our current understanding of quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in solar and stellar chromospheres. Following a definition of QPPs and a brief overview of their historical development, we discuss various QPP categories, detection methods, and potential physical mechanisms. We then review the latest findings on QPPs in both solar and stellar chromospheres, highlighting recent breakthroughs and emerging trends in this area of research. Notably, certain patterns of QPPs in both types of chromospheres exhibit intriguing similarities. Future investigation of QPPs will likely prioritize in-depth analysis of these mechanisms and more detailed comparisons between solar and stellar observations.

This research introduces an anomaly detection method based on a self-attention mechanism within a deep convolutional neural network framework. The self-attention approach allows the model to concentrate on specific image regions that may indicate anomalies. These regions are identified by the network's ability to process various scales simultaneously, guided by a novel parameter that regulates the emphasis given to each scale. The proposed method is trained on images of a specific object without prior knowledge of its normal appearance, and its ability to recognize and localize anomalies in novel objects is demonstrated. The results show that the model's performance improves as the number of training objects increases, allowing for the detection of anomalies in objects from unseen domains.

This study investigates the well-posedness of a broad family of equations related to Kadomtsev--Petviashvili I, even in situations where initial data have low regularity. The equations under consideration are one-dimensional modifications of the original KP equation, incorporating $C^{\infty}$-smooth functions that apply nonlinear dispersion interactions. Notably, our research demonstrates the strong dispersion of KP-like equations leads to the stability of solutions in $H^s$ spaces for $s\geq 1/2$ within the Besov norm $E^s p \cap H^s$. Additionally, our findings show that for any given $s\geq 1/2$ and $p\geq 2$, a specific $L^2$-Sobolev norm of the dispersion term must be finite in order for the equation to have a unique solution within the Besov norm $E^s p \cap H^s$. This research also establishes the continuity of the flow generated by our equations within the Besov-Orlicz spaces.

Kramers' theorem has been extensively studied in various fermionic systems with a distinct energy spectrum. However, its application in non-hermitian systems with a more complex energy structure has received less attention. This paper delves into the inverse Kramers theorem in non-hermitian systems, specifically in two-dimensional finite lattices with degenerate edge states. By examining the symmetry properties of these systems, we can derive the conditions under which the inverse Kramers' theorem applies. Our research has important implications for designing non-hermitian systems with intriguing topological characteristics.

A novel channel estimation method is introduced for systems with massive MIMO and OFDM, particularly designed to handle high user mobility by leveraging a deep learning-based channel prediction framework. The approach involves online prediction of the channel state using historical data at the transmitter, informed by estimated delay and channel length, which is updated with measured received signals to prevent prediction drift. As a result, a reduced number of pilot symbols can be employed, utilizing a two-stage least squares channel estimation technique. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance over the conventional pilot based estimation method under high mobility conditions.

This research develops a statistical approach to accurately determine regional income disparities with a specified level of precision, suitable for spatial analysis across various scales. Employing a multilevel model combined with a spatial error structure, the method provides an effective framework for estimating the degree of spatial dependence in income inequality. Furthermore, the study incorporates a Bayesian estimation technique along with two adaptive smoothing methods to account for diverse data patterns and incorporates a post-processing step to enhance estimation precision. Through simulations and applications using German and Portuguese regional data, the efficacy of this approach is demonstrated.

We define the Grauert tube of a real-analytic manifold as $M_\tau$ with radius $\tau$, along with its associated projectors, and establish a key boundary integral of the Szeg{\o} projector in this context. By leveraging this boundary operator, we demonstrate a maximum principle governing CR functions on the Grauert tube, with implications for a boundary Stokes theorem. Furthermore, this boundary operator plays a crucial role in proving a theorem on positive Toeplitz operators, with specific applications to embedding problems and embedding theorem formulations for Grauert tubes.

We introduce the MARINLINGA algorithm, an efficient implementation of Boivin and Boesch's reverse line graph algorithm using adjacency lists. This algorithm achieves a worst-case time complexity of O(n+ε) and includes a modified approach to improve its practical performance. Building upon the MARINLINGA algorithm, we also develop the MARINLINEGRAPH algorithm, which enables the creation of the reverse line graph of a line graph in O(n+ε) time. To further extend the concept, we propose a family of algorithms, the MARINLINEGRAPH-i.h algorithm, which allows the construction of the i-th line graph power of a given graph G in O(n) time.

This paper validates Lee-Lee's hypothesis by demonstrating an equivalence between the roots associated with non-self-intersecting curves in an affine framework and real Schur roots within an acyclic quiver. Consequently, this finding offers an alternative, quiver-theoretic, proof of the Garsia-Mingus-Lecuona's sign-hook formula.

In modern software development, applications are comprised of numerous dependent modules that draw on existing libraries. To maintain this complex framework, developers often rely on code review systems. Unfortunately, a significant proportion of these dependencies prove to be redundant or excessively large, hindering application maintenance and development efficiency. To address this challenge, a novel approach called DepRed is introduced, designed to identify and eliminate unnecessary dependencies within dependent modules through the application of machine learning algorithms. By evaluating dependency importance based on commit history, changelog records, and code activity, DepRed accurately distinguishes between essential and redundant dependencies. Experimental validation on real-world open-source projects demonstrates that DepRed effectively distinguishes between vital and non-vital dependencies (F1-score: 83.33%), and a notable reduction in unnecessary dependencies can be achieved through its implementation (62.5% decrease).

In the following study, the entanglement between two fictional polymer chains is analyzed through time-series data obtained from simulations of interacting polymer chains with shared points of attachment. The series of values representing the degree of similarity between the chains is examined and it is determined that this degree of similarity follows a pattern that can be described as a fractional Brownian motion with a mean reversion component. A mathematical formula describing this phenomenon is developed, and it is found that this formula effectively describes the results from both the simulation and physical experiment performed.

To tackle complex optimization problems with uncertain relationships and intense computational loads, we develop a method that breaks down challenging problems into more manageable components. Our approach involves dividing the challenging problem into simpler subproblems and a higher-level problem that guides the solution of the subproblems through a set of scenario paths. We then use a specialized algorithm to efficiently calculate a key distributional robustness property, allowing each guided subproblem to incorporate multiple possible outcomes from uncertain relationships. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a scheduling problem in a flexible manufacturing system, and we show that it produces near-optimal solutions to the original problem.

This paper introduces a novel approach for future video feature generation and action anticipation through a time-series framework. Differing from the common practice of isolating a single action, our method aims to model sequences of actions by utilizing a Recurrent Neural Network with Look-Ahead. By leveraging this architecture, we demonstrate its ability to effectively predict not only individual future actions but also subsequent actions in a video sequence. The recurrent neural network's output is a sequence of action probabilities, which are then filtered using a threshold to indicate whether an action has commenced. The length of the look-ahead horizon is dynamically determined based on the output threshold. The method's efficacy is further amplified by integrating a temporal coherence module, which ensures that generated action sequences adhere to a logical order. The approach's performance was validated through its exceptional results on the EPIC-KITCHENS and Sub-Kitchen datasets.

We explore the emergence of a deep thermalization phase in closed quantum many-body systems, where the entire Hilbert space converges to a macroscopic superposition of microstates. Our research identifies a clear boundary distinguishing the deep thermalization regime from conventional equilibrium or nonequilibrium states. Specifically, we propose a criterion for deep thermalization based on the average duration of a quantum measurement. Furthermore, we outline a theoretical and experimental approach for generating and verifying the deep thermalization phase.

We prove the conditions under which pseudo-differential operators function within the framework of homogeneous trees, leveraging a characterization of homogeneous trees via their compact one-point topological group actions to establish this. Furthermore, we apply this result to address questions pertaining to the boundedness of localized pseudo-differential operators and associated operator families.

The increasing use of 5G technology has significantly increased human 5G electromagnetic field exposure, which is being researched to minimize potential health risks. To study this, we analyzed the spatial distribution of 6G research nodes and 5G radio base stations in an urban area using their GPS coordinates and found that users' 6G exposure is lower than 5G exposure. Due to the high penetration of 6G devices in everyday life, we then estimated the total 6G exposure, which revealed that users are exposed to higher 6G field levels than radio base stations. As a result, we suggest that 6G research should prioritize measuring and assessing the effects of 6G-related electromagnetic fields on humans' health.

Deep neural networks tend to make inaccurate predictions outside their known data distribution. However, it's possible for these networks to confidently misidentify samples as in-domain rather than making a more realistic uncertain prediction. We propose a straightforward technique, Conditional Output Discriminators (CODEs), to address this issue. CODEs utilize the network's final layer and a two-player min-max game to learn how to distinguish between in-domain and out-of-distribution samples. We then utilize this knowledge to modify the network's final layer to promote more accurate predictions. Our experiments show that modifying the final network layer to promote uncertain predictions significantly improves out-of-distribution performance on multiple datasets and settings.

High-energy proton-proton collisions, particularly those occurring at 13 TeV, have been extensively studied via 108 or 110 TeV azimuthal jet correlations to evaluate sensitivity to various underlying theories, such as quantum gravity and high-energy perturbative QCD. Calculations have been performed for both 108 and 110 TeV cases, incorporating leading and next-to-leading order perturbative QCD corrections, as well as the effects of soft gluon resummation at next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. It is found that incorporating these corrections significantly enhances the sensitivity of next-to-leading logarithmic calculations to quantum gravity's impact at a scale of G, which is the Planck constant.

Deep learning models have achieved impressive breakthroughs in various tasks, particularly in computer vision and natural language processing. However, the extensive need for large labeled training datasets, which are expensive to acquire, severely limits the practicality of these models. To overcome this significant challenge, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques have been developed to maximize data utility for deep model training. This study provides a comprehensive overview of these approaches, focusing on representation learning, particularly for image data. Recent advances in semi-supervised and unsupervised learning, including contrastive learning and self-supervised learning, have shown promising results in closing the performance gap with supervised learning in several computer vision tasks. This study offers an in-depth analysis of these approaches, discussing their underlying principles, architectures, and training methods. Additionally, it examines the impact of training data on the effectiveness of these techniques, providing an overview of their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, it reviews the current state of semi-supervised learning for image classification, segmentation, and generation, highlighting the potential of semi-supervised learning to make a major contribution in computer vision, particularly in handling the scarcity of labelled data.

Anomaly detection in tabular datasets, which involves identifying unusual data patterns, is a complex problem due to the large number of potential anomalies. To address this issue, we present a new method that uses a neural network to generate features representing the reconstruction errors of various distance measures. These error features are then combined using an aggregation function, which we find improves upon the simple summation of their individual distances. We have tested this approach on multiple datasets, comparing its efficacy against established benchmarks, and the results show that incorporating reconstruction error features enhances the performance of anomaly detection methods. Furthermore, our feature-based approach outperforms or matches the performance of state-of-the-art anomaly detection techniques while offering greater flexibility in adapting to different distance measures and aggregation strategies.

This paper begins by establishing a fundamental theorem that confirms the existence and uniqueness of a classical mild solution in a broad non-linear equation framework. Leveraging this core theorem, we subsequently derive and demonstrate various key properties of the solution set and derive essential estimates. Furthermore, we expand on our research findings by examining an equation system that represents a modified Generalized KdV-Burgers model.

We examine how neutrinos interact with light (pseudo)scalar mediators, which then couple to photons. This process generates observable signals in experiments like BLAZE, HPS, and R&D experiments such as BEPC-II and CEPC, which are analogous to the HELIX and HELIOS proposals. We propose specific collider experiment setups to constrain and discover the proposed light (pseudo)scalar mediators, which is then applied to the specific case of the BEPC-II collider.

The significance of interactions between neurons and glial cells in the brain has been observed to influence the activity of neural networks. However, incorporating these interactions into complex biological models is a difficult task due to the lack of detailed knowledge about their mechanisms. The following research explores how such interactions can be modeled in large-scale networks, focusing on a specific aspect: how glial cells can affect the synaptic connections between neurons. A key finding is that a common mathematical model of glial cells can be related to a common model of plasticity in synaptic connections. The research also examines the conditions under which the two models are equivalent and suggests that the similarity may not be coincidental. A further study is proposed to examine how the glial model can be used to explain how a neural network develops over time, taking into account changes in the strength of synaptic connections.

In a study of a theoretical model, a particle interacts with two distinct magnetic fields within a confined space, resulting in the particle displaying unique behavior when passing through, characterized by interference patterns and distinct probability heat signatures. This research provides a novel platform for studying quantum properties such as wave-particle duality and interference, potentially paving the way for the application in quantum information technology.

We investigate how quickly a particular event occurs in the diffusion of a particle that occasionally encounters a moving barrier. This barrier is randomly positioned and moves at a constant speed. The study focuses on the time it takes for the particle to reach the barrier for the $n$th time and find the associated probability distribution. Interestingly, we discover that the likelihood of this event occurring within a specific timeframe of $t$ is inversely proportional to $2^{n-1}$ times a function that increases linearly with $t$, and decreases polynomially with $t$.

For a comprehensive understanding, it is crucial to examine the structure of the formal semigroups associated with the Alexander polynomials of a specific type of knot known as L-space knots. The main objective of this study is to establish a comprehensive ordering of the formal semigroups related to Alexander polynomials of a particular subset of torus knots, which are a special type of L-space knot. It is noteworthy that the classification of these formal semigroups has significant implications for determining the genus of certain types of links, specifically braids with two strands.

We examine the long-term behavior of a system consisting of a rotating heat conducting fluid in a three-dimensional domain with smooth boundaries. Under the influence of gravitational pull in the direction of rotation, the fluid's evolution is governed by the Navier-Stokes equations with time-varying viscosity. As viscosity approaches zero, the system's dynamics converge to the Euler equations. Our research shows that, over a short to medium-term timeframe, the system's solutions align with those of a related Euler equation. Notably, the solution can develop intricate patterns, including those with alternating vorticity and strength, as well as rotational characteristics. Our findings extend to solutions featuring sharp gradients.

In this research, we introduce a novel deep-learning method that uses an ensemble approach to enhance the performance of object detection. By combining the strengths of several deep models, each with distinct characteristics, our approach effectively reduces the negative effects of overfitting patterns that emerge during training. Our ensemble method, termed SAV, consists of a hierarchical structure that combines two types of decision-making layers: those that aggregate decisions at an image level and those that aggregate inferences across a network of models. SAV's individual components are designed to minimize overfitting, each utilizing a unique loss function and trained separately. Our results, obtained through extensive experimentation with the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset, demonstrate the superior effectiveness of our approach compared to leading state-of-the-art object detection methods.

Code is composed of various types of identifiers, which are labeled with generic names like class, attribute, and method labels. These labels reflect the structure of the code's abstract syntax tree. In this study, we analyze the naming conventions of identifiers in a large dataset of Python code to identify patterns and assess the effectiveness of name analysis in automatically generating labels for similar code. Our findings indicate that identifier names are often short, use single words, and can be categorized into distinct groups. A designed model can leverage these patterns to accurately predict labels for identifiers.

Let $\mathbb{K}$ be an arbitrary field that is closed under scalars of degree 2 or more.  We analyze the unital, associative algebra $A=\algebra(NIL)$, which consists of polynomials in the indeterminates $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ over $\mathbb{K}$.  An element $a$ of $A$ is classified as a NIL vector if it is a linear combination of monomials of degree 2 or greater.  We prove that the set of NIL vectors forms a subalgebra within $A$, and we derive a generating set for this subset.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the set of NIL vectors is a right, left, and two-sided solvable algebra, and we identify the maximal subalgebra within $A$.  We also prove that the set of NIL vectors is a right, left, and two-sided Hopf subalgebra, and we derive a formula for its dual.  Finally, we demonstrate that the set of NIL vectors is a right, left, and two-sided Hopf subalgebra, and we prove that its dual is isomorphic to the original set.

The development of intricate microstructures, such as those found in composites like Cu-Zn, has long been a subject of interest due to their unique properties and complex grain structures. The growth dynamics of these structures, comprising multiple phases, are poorly understood, yet the process of grain growth provides valuable insights into their evolution. Our investigation into the grain growth of a Cu-Zn alloy, with a primary grain size of 50 $\mu$m, reveals that the average grain growth of the two constituent phases, while influenced by their interactions, is primarily driven by isotropic grain growth. Notably, the growth of the larger grain in each phase dominates that of the smaller grain, and the development of new grain boundaries significantly accelerates the overall growth process. Our study also examines the impact of secondary grain growth, leading to the formation of complex microstructures, and demonstrates that the final microstructure can be best explained by a combination of isotropic grain growth and preferred interaction between specific grain types. Our findings offer new insights into the intricate grain growth processes in complex microstructures, which can be applied to other multi-phase systems.

Human pose and shape estimation from images is a fundamental problem in computer vision that has seen rapid advancements in recent years, largely driven by the availability of large-scale multi-person datasets. Despite these progress gains, current methods often rely on a single type of data, leading to performance limitations when encountering new and unfamiliar human poses or environments. To address this limitation, we present a new paradigm that leverages multiple datasets and learns to generalize across data boundaries using a novel method of training with a generated pseudo-label. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on a range of evaluation tasks.

In a dilute electron system with an abundance of negatively charged U-centers, our research indicates that superconductivity emerges due to an effective electron-electron attraction. This phenomenon arises from the scattering of electrons off positively charged atoms at low temperatures, generating a residual attractive force mediating the electron interaction. Utilizing the Bardeen-Pines model, we calculate the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) and find that it is significantly influenced by the negatively charged impurities. Notably, a relatively simple expression enables the estimation of $T_c$ in relation to the concentration of negatively charged impurities, closely aligning with experimental findings for cadmium-doped strontium. This study offers new insights into the role of negatively charged impurities in the formation of superconductivity.

We've conducted a global fit of all relevant observable outcomes from the LHC's 13 TeV data, covering nearly 140 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, to assess the sensitivity of different collider processes and their combined constraints on new physics. Our primary focus lies on constraints derived from the tree-level signal of scalar leptoquarks. We discovered that a comprehensive analysis of diverse processes, such as single top production, top color processes, W boson pair production, electroweak production of the Higgs boson, associated charm production, and quark resonance searches, is necessary to accurately evaluate the implications of new physics. Our findings indicate that a complete simulation of these processes within the Standard Model is feasible with current data, and that a straightforward extrapolation of results from single process fits to the global fit is unreliable. Notably, the overall fit reveals a significant improvement in the sensitivity to new physics, with a minimum integrated luminosity of 100 fb$^{-1}$ required for optimal results.

Machine learning has become ubiquitous in various fields, yet the mathematical underpinnings of its applications in these domains are not always apparent to those outside the academic community. The intersection of category theory and machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years, with researchers from both fields now collaborating to shed light on the underlying mathematical concepts. This paper provides an overview of the growing intersection between category theory and machine learning.

This paper explores the control problem for Newton's motion dynamics, focusing on the terminal sliding mode control approach. To address this issue, we develop a new dynamic output error regression (DOER) framework, which incorporates the available output state information in a way that utilizes the measurable component to its maximum potential, ensuring optimal power usage according to Newton's second-order motion dynamics. The proposed DOER framework is then integrated into a robust terminal sliding mode control scheme to enhance the robustness against external disturbances and ensure fast convergence of the state trajectories to the equilibrium point. The stability and convergence of the proposed control scheme are mathematically proven, accompanied by simulation studies that validate the theoretical findings.

Lithium-ion batteries are crucial components in numerous technologies that rely on renewable energy. The growing significance of these technologies has increased the demand for advanced, non-destructive evaluation techniques to monitor the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries. In this study, a highly innovative and low-cost method using ultrasonic resonant properties is proposed to monitor the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries without causing damage. The results show that the thickness and resonant frequencies can effectively monitor the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries. The findings of this study suggest that the presented method has great potential for monitoring the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries.

This study presents a new approach to tracking control for gantry crane that uses discrete-time methods, offering improved real-world application potential compared to traditional continuous-time approaches. By incorporating a measure of position and velocity, the error between the load's desired and actual path can be accurately quantified. A novel sliding mode control strategy is developed to stabilize the system, featuring a specific disturbance and filter approach. Through Lyapunov stability analysis, it is demonstrated that the proposed control strategy results in finite time convergence of tracking errors. Additionally, practical considerations such as saturation limits are addressed to ensure robustness in the control system. Finally, simulation results confirm the superior performance of the new control method compared to alternative approaches.

Significant improvements in image captioning systems have been achieved through large, high-quality caption datasets created by human contributors. However, these datasets are often expensive to produce, leading researchers to explore methods that can help reduce their size without compromising performance. A novel approach in this area is shown to be effective by a new technique called multi-source filtering, which can be applied to existing datasets to optimize them for better performance. By combining multiple diversity metrics, this method helps identify the most valuable captions that should be retained in the optimized dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that optimizing MSHuman50D, a large captioning dataset, results in a more efficient dataset with similar or better performance on several evaluation metrics.

Let's define a collection of strings $\mathcal{L}$ and a positive integer $k$. We say a set of $k$ disjoint subsets $\{S_1,\ldots,S_k\}$ from $\mathcal{L}$ is well-connected if for any $1\leq i\leq k$ and any $1\leq j\ < \ i$, there exists a string $w$ within $\mathcal{L}$ whose $j$-th substring is equal to $w$'s $j-1$th substring and its $i$-th substring is equal to $w$'s $i$-th substring. The problem of determining the complexity of identifying well-connected collections of strings is considered. We present a solution for this problem by showing that it belongs to the NC^2 class of complexity. We achieve this through a method that converts the problem into a solution of systems of linear equations, where each equation has a constant number of equations and variables.

Ehresmann semigroups can be considered as a broader extension of monoids.
Ordered Ehresmann semigroups are characterized by their internal order relation.
This study focuses on two specific types: left-increasing and right-increasing ordered Ehresmann semigroups.
The research includes a discussion of their fundamental characteristics.

Recent advancements in self-attention architectures have led to remarkable performance improvements across various natural language processing tasks. Notwithstanding these achievements, the underlying reasons behind the effectiveness of these models remain unclear. To shed light on this, our investigation focuses on the impact of network geometry on the expressiveness of self-attention architectures. Specifically, we demonstrate that the computational power of these models is directly tied to their width and depth. Moreover, we show that optimizing the network's geometry for a specific task yields results comparable to highly complex models, potentially reducing computational expenses.

This research investigates the efficacy of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles as a visible light photocatalyst, particularly in the degradation of methyl orange. The nanoparticles were synthesized through hydrothermal hydrolysis in water at two temperatures: 170 $^{o}$C and 180 $^{o}$C. Characterization via X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed the nanoparticles' single-phase presence, rhombohedral structure, and iron content. UV-visible absorption spectroscopy revealed that these nanoparticles exhibited a direct transition and could potentially be used as visible light photocatalysts. Visible light photocatalytic experiments using the nanoparticles showed that their efficiency in degrading methyl orange was greater than that of the bulk material. This enhanced performance can be attributed to the higher surface area of the nanoparticles, which was confirmed through thermogravimetric analysis. Furthermore, the effect of the nanoparticles' size on the photocatalytic performance was examined and the results demonstrated that BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles of 20 nm in size were the most effective.

A model is developed to explain the properties of the light Higgs particle, as well as the characteristics of the 125 GeV Higgs boson discovered at the Large Hadron Collider. This model involves a single "flipped" electroweak sector, supplemented by a distinct $SU(2)_H$ gauge group, which also incorporates a separate Higgs doublet, referred to as $\Phi_2$. Within the context of this model, the vacuum expectation value of the first Higgs doublet, $\Phi_1$, breaks the electroweak symmetry, while the second Higgs doublet, $\Phi_2$, does not. We introduce a set of new fermions to break the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, leading to a gauge theory that is anomaly-free and features a distinct $SU(2)_H$ gauge symmetry. We investigate the properties of the electroweak symmetry breaking and the Higgs boson properties through the matching of the Higgs effective Lagrangian at tree level. We also investigate the potential of the upcoming HL-LHC to detect the properties of the light Higgs boson and the $W'_{}$ gauge boson, as well as the heavy top-like quarks, by analyzing the potential signals and experimental reach through a comprehensive simulation of the ATLAS experiment.

In this research, we address the challenge of predicting a hand-held object's geometry from a single RGB image, given the object is grasped by a hand with varying grasping positions. A novel approach, HandArtiNet, is proposed to tackle this challenge, incorporating both hand and object features into a unified reconstruction framework. A hand- and object-aware convolutional neural network is designed to capture their interaction and produce a hand-centric representation, enabling accurate scale estimation and hand articulation detection. This information is then utilized to generate a 3D object volume by a fully connected network, taking into account the hand's articulation. Comprehensive experiments on the HandX-1.1K dataset demonstrate that HandArtioNet achieves superior performance over current methods. Moreover, our approach is successfully applied to the task of hand object manipulation, given sufficient training data.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) has successfully captured high-resolution spectra of the Sun's outer atmosphere at an unprecedented level of detail. Utilizing the Fort Davis system, a specialized ALMA receiver designed to observe the Sun's Ca-K line, we conducted a comprehensive study using advanced techniques. Our research involved comparing ALMA's Ca-K line data to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/Space Weather Service's historical records and to the data obtained through the High Resolution Spectrograph on the Solar Dynamics Observatory. The results show significant improvement in Ca-K line data correlation after applying the Equal Contrast technique, which considers variations in intensity. Furthermore, we found that the shape of the Ca-K line core aligns well with the total intensity data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, but the line core width from ALMA surpasses this similarity. Our findings suggest that the Ca-K line data from ALMA are highly reliable and potentially the most trustworthy among existing observational methods.

The search for Sigma-plus decaying into the proton-antiproton pi-plus and for other specific two-body decay modes was conducted using 460 pb^-1 of proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb detector at 7 TeV. No notable excess was observed in the majority of investigated channels. However, an observed 4.4 standard deviation excess in the specified decay of Sigma-plus to proton-antiproton pi-plus with specific kinematic constraints led to a constraint on the mass difference between the Lambda_c+b and Lambda_c+b masses, which was determined to be 141 +/- 35 MeV.

A conventional method for finding vulnerabilities through symbolic execution is limited by its synchronous nature, making it less effective for testing complex programs that have multiple execution paths. This limitation is overcome by new techniques presented in this paper, called distributed symbolic execution, and they produce performance comparable to or better than sequential execution, especially for long test runs. These techniques employ test-depth partitioning to divide program paths among asynchronous agents and synchronize their progress through a hierarchical synchronization mechanism based on shared data structures. This approach ensures that each agent maintains a consistent global understanding of program execution history and effectively resolves conflicts between agents. Testing can be further optimized by distributing paths randomly and using a work-list-based method to identify any resulting performance bottlenecks. Evaluations of these techniques have shown significant improvements in speed compared to sequential execution, especially for long test runs, and their effectiveness has been demonstrated on various commercial codebases.

The magnetic relaxation data of single magnetically blocked magnetic nanoparticles and ensembles with varying sizes and interparticle interactions have been simulated using a stochastic magnetic dynamics model. This model calculates the magnetic moment relaxation data of single nanoparticles and ensembles with different parameters. It is found that the aspect ratio of the nanoparticles affects the relaxation curve and time range where dipolar interactions have a noticeable impact. Ensemble nanoparticles with a low size variation show relaxation behavior that depends on the properties of the individual nanoparticles, rather than the collective effects.

A new paradigm in machine learning, Federated Learning (FL) has been widely adopted for preserving data security and supports a range of learning algorithms. However, in a multi-agent setting, where a network of FL agents collaboratively learns from shared data, there exists a significant challenge in balancing fairness and fairness-awareness among the agents. In such a network, where each agent possesses a unique model, computes gradients, and updates models, achieving fairness in a way that accounts for fairness-awareness becomes crucial. Leveraging the concept of $k$-median clustering, we introduce a novel framework, FairFed, which enables a collection of FL agents to learn in a fair and privacy-conscious manner. By incorporating fairness-awareness into the aggregation of gradients and model updates, FairFed provides a robust solution. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of FairFed in delivering accurate and fair models while maintaining a satisfactory level of generalization performance.

Recent neural network-based approaches have achieved impressive results in short-text classification tasks, however, they are often unable to effectively utilize contextual information in subsequent documents of a sequence. To address this, we propose a method that integrates a recurrent neural network within a transformer framework. This enables our model to leverage the contextual knowledge from previous documents to enhance its classification performance, which we have successfully demonstrated by achieving a new state-of-the-art performance on the Stanford Natural Language Understanding dataset.

Recent research on Fabry-Pérot etalons has highlighted the complex relationship between structural parameters and electric field enhancements. This paper presents a comprehensive two-dimensional sensitivity analysis, using the perturbation approach, to examine how variations in optical thickness or refractive index index change the electric field. The research focuses specifically on thin-film agitated double Fabry-Pérot etalons, and a mathematical expression is developed to estimate the electric field modification caused by index changes. The study evaluates the effectiveness of this modification in enhancing the electric field and examines how adjusting the spacing between the interfering plates influences this enhancement. The research also considers the impact of index enhancement in thin films on the results, and a comparison is made with alternative enhancement techniques. The ultimate goal of this research is to provide a practical framework for designing Fabry-Pérot etalons with enhanced electric fields.

A compatible matching in multiple labeled point sets is possible if all points within sets are labeled, such that no two points share the same label and their spatial proximity corresponds to their label proximity.  It is proven that no more than n compatible matchings can be found in sets of n labeled points, a result that extends a previous theorem for two sets.  When comparing sets of three or more points, a more complex measure of compatibility applies, taking into account the points' spatial arrangement, but a proof shows that no more than n compatible matchings can be found in sets of size n.  This result relies on a previously established theorem concerning the probability of a tree's construction through a series of random edges.

The next generation of deep learning accelerators is expected to be built upon specialized hardware accelerators. However, the complexity of these systems will make it difficult to integrate them with multiple vendor components, requiring innovative system-level approaches to overcome scalability and integration challenges. A new technology, chiplet architecture, has been proposed to address these limitations by allowing distinct functional dies to be combined into a single die. This study introduces the first large-scale deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) accelerator designed using chiplet technology, which integrates a 256 x 256 image tile and 32 filters in a single unit. The design is implemented using TSMC's 5nm process, resulting in a 0.45mm^2 die size that is approximately five times larger than a previous state-of-the-art CNN accelerator built using the same process in a 4x4 array. The design also enables the construction of extremely large CNNs, such as those with 1024 x 1024 image tiles and 1024 filters in a single die, which is a significant improvement over the state-of-the-art. The study also compares the design's area and power consumption with a previous accelerator built using the same process in a 4x4 array and estimates the design's scalability to larger image tiles and more cores.

In survival analysis, mixture cure models are used to estimate the proportion of the population that remains disease-free. They also provide an estimate of the population fraction that experiences the disease. Existing models typically assume that the disease-free and affected populations respond to treatment differently, which can be costly to research. Our study introduces a new treatment response model that assumes individuals are homogeneous in their response to treatment across all groups. We develop parametric and non-parametric methods for this model based on this assumption. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our model produces more accurate estimates of treatment effect than existing models, making it suitable for use in real-world data. Our method is particularly useful for applications involving multiple treatment groups.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph, denoted by $\bar{dim}_N(G)$, is the smallest size of a set of vertices, where any two distinct vertices are at a distance differing by at least some positive integer value, if such value exists. We examine the nonlocal metric dimension of specific graph classes including generalized cubes, power domination trees, particular subgraphs of Cartesian products, and full bipartite graphs. We enhance a known formula for computing the nonlocal metric dimension of complete $n$-partite graphs and provide a conjecture extending this to complete bipartite graphs.

In-memory computing systems have shown great promise in speeding up computations, particularly with complex models like deep neural networks. However, a major drawback of using these systems is the high power consumption when there are fewer inputs to process, resulting in underutilized hardware. To counteract this, a new hybrid approach, called MemPad, has been developed. By incorporating virtual padding, or artificial inputs with predetermined values, into data streams that are being processed in real-time, a significant amount of energy can be saved. This is achieved as the amount of padding increases, allowing a more balanced distribution of computations to take place. The proposed system, MemPad, has been tested on widely used deep neural network models across multiple benchmark datasets. The results show that using MemPad leads to increased hardware utilization and a significant reduction in energy consumption without compromising model performance. Notably, MemPad's efficiency is particularly evident in tasks where there are numerous redundant features, resulting in substantial power savings. Overall, a key advantage of MemPad is the ability to automatically and dynamically adjust to varying computation volumes without any modification to the model or hardware architecture.

This study introduces a method for creating shorter polar codes with improved performance through the use of reduced-size polarization kernels. To address the computational complexity of generating polar codes on a large scale, the researchers propose an algorithm to systematize the construction of smaller polar codes using standard components. Their method relies on finding suitable building blocks that approximate the properties of the original large polar code. To achieve this, the researchers establish specific criteria for the components based on the characteristics of the original polar code. As a result, they developed shorter polarization kernels that perform better than standard polar codes under adverse channel conditions. To support their findings, the researchers evaluated the performance of these shorter polar codes under the polarized Gaussian discrete input channel, demonstrating that they match the performance of longer polar codes with a significant reduction in the number of bits they encode.

A novel approach to removing noise from seismic data, utilizing deep denoising transformers, has been introduced. The method, trained on artificial noise-free data, demonstrates impressive performance, outdoing previously established techniques. However, the reliance on high-quality training data limits its effectiveness. To mitigate this, we propose an alternative strategy, where a supervised deep learning model is paired with a self-supervised transformer to refine its capabilities. The self-supervised model's denoising skills are then transferred to enhance the performance of the initial model. The outcome is a more resilient method, capable of achieving superior results even when trained on inferior data. The developed approach demonstrates its value in applying deep learning to real-world data, marked by its success in processing the large-scale deepwater Gulf of Mexico seismic dataset.

Researchers investigate the effects of a two-photon exchange in lepton-nucleon scattering by analyzing the difference in lepton angular distributions and the dispersion of lepton energy. The data from experiments that measure the difference in lepton distributions and the dispersion of lepton energy are combined and compared to lepton-scattering cross section measurements. The cross section data from several experiments including the Hall A measurements from studies like PVEX and PCEX are analyzed. The lepton energy covered in these analyses spans from a few MeV to 6 GeV, enabling researchers to explore the potential presence of higher timelike resonances such as the f2(1570) and the f2'(1760). The results obtained from these analyses reveal that the lepton energy and the lepton flavor have a significant influence on the cross section and the lepton energy dispersion. The data also indicate that the cross section and the lepton energy dispersion exhibit a similar behavior in lepton-proton and the neutron scattering. The lepton energy dispersion data from lepton-nucleus scattering are also analyzed and compared to the lepton-proton scattering results. The results from these analyses reveal that the lepton-nucleus scattering data are consistent with the lepton-proton scattering results and the lepton energy dispersion data from Hall A are consistent with the lepton-nucleon scattering data from Jefferson Lab. The lepton-nucleus data from the lepton energy dispersion are also compared to the lepton-nucle

We're investigating the behavior of electrons or holes in antiferromagnetic lattices under the influence of a robust on-site Coulomb interaction. This scenario is commonly observed in magnetic materials with doped charge carriers, such as half-metallic ferromagnets, spin-density wave materials, and doped Mott insulators. The energy required for the system to reach a state of charge neutrality is substantial. As a result, the system naturally aligns itself in a striped pattern, which is characterized by long stripes that span multiple layers. This striped pattern can be preserved over long distances due to the system's ability to form a striped superlattice. This study provides a detailed analysis of the system's properties, including its magnetic and electronic characteristics, and offers a new perspective on the system's behavior. This perspective is supported by numerical simulations and a simplified model that describe the system's behavior at low temperatures.

Researchers studying various applications aim to quantify direct and indirect
causal relationships. A widely used approach, mediation analysis, aims to
understand these connections in a given causal framework but is not suitable for
non-parametric models. In this context, we introduce an objective causal
modeling technique that allows for independent mediation analysis through multiple
paths, and demonstrate its application in estimating direct and indirect
causal relationships. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data show that
our proposed approach surpasses existing methods in multiple settings.

A starshade is a large space telescope companion designed to block starlight by creating a narrow gap between a telescope and nearby celestial objects. This concept involves using a rigid, three-dimensional structure made of thin panels that can be adjusted to reach the ideal shape for optimal operation. To achieve this, engineers need to develop advanced methods for constructing the frame system, determining the ideal shape for maximum performance, and designing mechanisms to maintain the required angle and shape. To address these challenges, researchers have developed a theoretical framework for calculating the ideal shape, a simulation method for predicting system performance, a simulation tool for analyzing and optimizing mechanical system behavior, and a computer-aided design tool for creating detailed mechanical component designs. To validate these approaches, engineers analyzed a full-scale starshade model and compared the results with simulations and in-slab measurements.

The detection of suicidal thoughts is a critical public health issue. Current research into predictive models has shown some promise, yet these models are rarely used in real-world settings. This study aims to improve the detection of suicidal thoughts by applying machine learning techniques to data collected from individuals not under medical supervision. A comparison of traditional machine learning methods with a cutting-edge artificial intelligence technique called a Transformer is conducted to determine the most effective approach for early detection. Our results suggest that the Transformer model performs better than conventional machine learning models, achieving an impressive 83.8% accuracy in detecting suicidal thoughts. The potential for these models to be used in real-world applications, enhancing crisis intervention, and improving public health services is highlighted.

This research explores the characteristics of supersymmetric Schwarzians, which is a way to describe superconformal groups, and demonstrates that they can represent two-dimensional superfield actions that are conformally invariant, and more generally, they can be used to describe conformal random fields in two dimensions, which reduces to describing Gaussian superfree fields in flat signature and to describing Gaussian fermionic and bosonic free fields in Euclidean signature.

The paper presents a new approach for numerically approximating solutions to discrete and continuous dynamical systems, and both qualitative and quantitative analyses can be performed. This is achieved through a symbolic and efficient algorithm that incorporates interval arithmetic, which sets a firm upper limit on errors. To illustrate the potential of the proposed method, it is applied to a range of systems, including the logistic map, the Lorenz system, and the Lotka-Volterra model.

We investigate non-linear solutions of the Einstein equations combined with a non-linear electrodynamics theory, specifically the Born-Infeld model, and examine both static and dynamical scenarios. In the static case, we derive a spherically symmetric spacetime with a power law relationship between energy density and the radial distance, and a central perfect fluid core surrounded by a non-linear magnetic field.
