Our study demonstrates the potential of spectroastrometry for studying the properties of deflector galaxies in quasar-lens systems, particularly the deflector's internal structure and the accretion of gas onto the supermass

This article focuses on the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a specific type of differential equation, known as the $q$-fractional differential equation, along with its associated boundary conditions. The main objective is to provide fundamental theory and consequences arising from this equation, as well as its solution via a reduction method. Furthermore, we establish inequalities for solutions that have specific bounds of $p$ and $\alpha$ values.

A broad framework is established to analyze the phonon Hall effect in dielectrics, utilizing a non-linear version of the Boltzmann equation that incorporates discrete crystal properties and the Berry phase, a quantum mechanical concept. Within this framework, we find that the phonon Hall conductivity is directly linked to the Berry curvature. The results show that the phonon Hall effect in solids can be influenced by the symmetry properties of the crystal structure and the discrete nature of the phonon modes. Specifically, we find that only Debye modes in monoclinic crystals are susceptible to the phonon Hall effect. The results from our framework are consistent with existing theories of the phonon Hall effect in lower symmetry crystals, as well as its absence in higher symmetry crystals.

A one-shot Raman imaging method utilizing the all-optical pump-probe setup in conjunction with lock-in autozeroing is demonstrated. This technique effectively eliminates both sample autofluvescence and external background and requires minimal sample handling and external equipment adjustments, allowing for quick positioning and focusing which takes less than one minute. The focused experiment presented in this paper showcases its capabilities in high-quality imaging of samples that aren't easily accessible.

This article focuses on deriving several complex inequalities for functions within the context of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities. Specifically, the investigation encompasses power and integral type inequalities incorporating max functions across multiple dimensions. Key findings include the introduction of multiple inequalities for sequences of partial sums of series with absolute values of harmonic functions within both one and two dimensions, as well as partial derivatives of harmonic functions within two dimensions.

In the context of the Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CTF) correspondence, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of black holes residing in Anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. We utilize the concept of conformal field theory (CTF) to calculate the mass and entropy of these black holes, which are derived from the AdS geometry. Our analysis is based on the first law of thermodynamics and the holographic principle. We then explore the thermodynamic behavior of multiple black holes and derive a formula for their total entropy. Subsequently, we examine the thermodynamic properties of a single black hole within a conformal field theory and explore the implications of its evaporation. Our research reveals that at the boundary black hole horizon, quantum effects lead to an increase in entropy, contradicting the second law of thermodynamics. This increase in entropy is attributed to the breakdown of the law of conservation of information at the horizon.

This research examines various measures of entropy - both modified and traditional - to identify distinct descendant states in two-dimensional Conformal Field Theory. We investigate the properties of these measures as they approach their limiting maximum values, equate to the Mathieu formula, and reach their minimum at the c/3 value. We introduce a novel approach to categorize conformal field theories using two-dimensional entanglement entropy. We also consider entropy derived from the modular Hamiltonian, including its regularization via dimensional regularization, to compare results with previous findings.

To evaluate the performance of control systems and validate the efficacy of cybersecurity solutions, researchers utilize Industrial Control System (ICS) testbeds. For advanced education, training, and collaborative research initiatives, existing testbeds provide valuable resources for scientific communities. Nonetheless, the continuous development of new technological solutions necessitates the creation of novel testbeds that incorporate the latest industrial equipment and cutting-edge communication protocols. This paper presents a novel ICS testbed, known as Edutubes, specifically designed to support research initiatives focused on human-machine interaction, human-centered design, and collaborative activities. The Edutubes testbed, comprising a simulated environment and a physical facility, leverages the integration of the Unity3D platform with an OPC-UA server to enable interaction between various platforms. The testbed's physical infrastructure, based on the same automation principles as the SIMuTUBES system, allows researchers to investigate and replicate the behavior of physical systems.

This study examines the challenges of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) when using methods that decompose rewards into a linear or monotonic form. We find that these methods are susceptible to issues arising from the limitations of their representation schemes. Specifically, when aiming for a linear solution, the required alignment between state features and optimal actions becomes increasingly stringent as the number of actions increases. Moreover, the necessary balance between state features and communication channels becomes highly complex when dealing with large or even moderately sized agent networks. We demonstrate that even simple agent configurations can lead to infeasible communication requirements for achieving the desired solution. Consequently, the agents must either employ unbounded communication or forgo essential state dependence, thereby compromising the effectiveness of the linear or monotonic decomposition. We propose an alternative approach based on the principles of information geometry and show that it can circumvent these representation limitations.

A common misconception, or "stereotype," often leads people to assume false connections between characteristics and traits of targeted groups. These misconceptions can result in negative outcomes, such as unfair treatment and exclusion. To address this issue, researchers have developed an automated method for stereotyping detection, involving the collection and analysis of large datasets, including the Stanford Sentiment Treebank and other text sources. By using a neural network to identify stereotypes, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in detecting stereotyping in human-annotated data, achieving accuracy rates comparable to established methods. Additionally, this study examines the impact of different linguistic and dependency relationships on stereotyping detection, providing further insights into this method's potential applications.

This study focuses on optimizing Remote Electrical Tilt (RET) settings for a Base Station serving multiple users in a heterogeneous wireless network. REMT allows for fine-tuning of remote radio head tilt and height to meet specific coverage requirements. In the context of downlink bandwidth-limited networks, our objective is to find the optimal tilt and height adjustments to minimize the number of users in need of power boost. To achieve this, we developed a new algorithm that builds upon the advanced Borshevkin, Chakravarti, and Ghosh approach for joint antenna tilt optimization. Our algorithm extends this framework to include height adjustments and applies a novel combinatorial optimization technique to find the optimal tilt and height settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing solutions, such as the Extended Multiuser Ratio OFDM approach for tilt optimization.

The average of three high-precision measurements of specific particle decays in the Tevatron collider led to a reliable estimate of a key CKM angle, resulting in a 3-sigma accuracy of 4.9 degrees and an 1-sigma error of 0.7 degrees.

Several properties of complex ellipsoids among convex bodies in n-dimensional space have been rigorously established in relation to their sections and projections. This research also employs complex transformations to extend the Reuleaux theorem and its complex counterpart, yielding various new inequalities for complex ellipsoids that are associated with specific properties, such as being cyclic, n-connected, or stable.

Current methods of collecting and sharing personal data are widely considered invasive,
typically viewed as unethical by the general public, and are a major cause of concern
regarding online security. People generally feel that they should have full control over
their private data and choose who it is shared with. A new approach, referred to as data
sovereignty, involves individuals having complete control over their personal data and
deciding how it is used and shared. Achieving true data sovereignty requires not only
secure protection of personal data but also accurate control over its usage. This paper
presents a groundbreaking, decentralized system that protects users' privacy and gives them
sovereignty over their data while also enabling them to monitor how it is used in a trustworthy
way. Our system has been tested with real users and real apps, demonstrating its effectiveness
in achieving data sovereignty and simplified usage control. A user-centric, modular design
is introduced, separating data protection and usage control, and incorporating a new, simple
mechanism for monitoring data usage in a decentralized manner.

A novel and efficient method for transmitting information through parallel
subchannels is presented, which can be applied to advanced communication systems
employing Faster-than-Nyquist signaling. The proposed method leverages the
capabilities of a low-rank matrix estimation tool to simultaneously decode
multiple streams of information. By utilizing the maximum amount of information
carried by each subchannel, the method achieves superior performance. The
developed joint detection scheme is then incorporated into a maximum likelihood
coded code division multiplexing system, which can be used to approximate the
performance of more complex systems, such as bit-interleaved coded modulation with trellis-coded modulation.

This study presents four distinct characterisations of a complete atomic lattice effect algebra, which must possess a particular combination of continuity and algebraic properties, to define it. We then establish a theory of interlocking (join-local-to-global) and fenchel (algebraic global-to-local) local elements within these complete atomic lattice effect algebras. In doing so, we arrive at a critical finding: every continuous lattice effect algebra is capable of being decomposed into a countable combination of locally finite, complemented and completely complemented subalgebras. As a direct result, we discover that every continuous lattice effect algebra may be represented as the local algebraic manifestation of a specific type of lattice function pair.

This research presents SaliencyMix, a reliable and efficient approach to enhancing the robustness of salient object detection models. Unlike previous methods, SaliencyMix data augments by blending input images with task-irrelevant regions, which are identified by relevant regions in the corresponding ground truth data. To prevent overfitting, this approach applies random masking to these regions. Our evaluation on the Cityscapes dataset and three leading salient object detection models shows that SaliencyMix is a superior data augmentation strategy, outperforming existing methods while requiring minimal resources. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/THUYENNGHOI/SaliencyMix.

We consider a specific category of matrices with complex entries that is analogous to the real special linear group and examine its group of bi-invariant functions. This leads to the establishment of three distinct convolution algebras, formed by bi-invariant functions within specified matrix groups. These algebras have properties such as being Fr\'echet spaces, non-commutative $C^*$-algebras and separating points, in addition to possessing specific functional calculus applications on the respective matrix groups.

The impact of galaxy shapes on the analysis of cosmic shear surveys is a significant source of error.  However, current analyses often overlook a crucial factor: the intrinsic correlation of galaxy shapes.  In this research, we investigate how these shape correlations affect the results of an experiment similar to the LSST survey, using a simulated dataset.  Our findings show that the most significant impact of shape correlations is on the detection of small, low-sensitivity patterns in the cosmic microwave background.  In order to effectively use the data from the LSST survey, it will be necessary to account for and correct for the intrinsic correlation of galaxy shapes.

In this study, we examine undercompressive behavior in soft-deformable particle systems and its implications for the stability of the associated Navier-Stokes systems. Through mathematical analysis, we reveal key differences in the dynamics of compressive versus non-compressive systems, indicating that the Navier-Stokes system associated with compressive behavior is thermodynamically non-unique. This analysis enables us to construct various smooth solutions to the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with significant differences in pressure and velocity. This phenomenon is specific to non-compressive conditions and does not affect the Navier-Stokes system's well-posedness in such scenarios.

To advance gold nanoparticles as a crucial material for quantum technologies, highly accurate computational models are necessary, but achieving this accuracy using experimental data alone is extremely challenging, often requiring years of time-resolved experiments at synchrotron radiation facilities. Therefore, developing reliable machine learning force fields to simulate gold nanoparticles is a key challenge. In this study, we propose a novel machine learning interatomic potential for gold, which enables the prediction of gold nanoparticles' structures and vibrational characteristics. By utilizing a combination of Gaussian Approximation Potentials and artificial neural networks with a wide range of features, including electronic density, we successfully demonstrate that our machine learning model surpasses conventional classical potentials in simulating gold dynamics. Our results indicate that this new approach can lead to a significant reduction in experimental data requirements, enabling the rapid design of gold nanoparticles with specific properties.

This is the beginning of a series that focuses on establishing various bifurcation theorems for a specific type of variational quasilinear elliptic problem with an arbitrary nonlinear term. Specifically, we are concerned with the equation -\mathcal{L}_0(u) = \lambda f(x,u)\; in\ \Omega, \; u=0 \; in\ \partial \Omega, where \mathcal{L}_0 is a uniformly elliptic operator and f(x,u) follows certain conditions, with $\Omega$ denoted as a bounded domain in \mathbb{R}^N. Our research draws from a notable paper by Vazquez and the subsequent work of Clapp and Peral, which investigated a semilinear version of this problem.

The observed fermion and lepton three-family system, which is part of a larger grand unification theory, is shown to be gauge-theoretically connected.  Within a non-mirrored SU(6) gauge framework, all three families share a common origin.  This includes a top quark and Higgs doublet that are generated through a spontaneous top-Higgs symmetry breaking process, which is made possible by the presence of an SU(2) subgroup.  This model is further developed to include spontaneous color symmetry breaking and a breakdown in the chiral U(1) family symmetry, both of which are driven by a common mechanism.  This results in the observed pattern of quark and lepton masses, and an overall vector-like structure.  This model is then compared to current data on lepton masses, mixing angles, and CP-violating phases, and is found to be consistent with experimental results.  It is also shown that the model is compatible with the existing limits on the Higgs particle's properties.
We derive from the associated q-Bernstein polynomials a novel expression for (h; q)-Genocchi numbers, which also yields a connection to the p-adic Bernoulli polynomials.

Randomized experiments are the gold standard for determining treatment effects, but they're only effective for short-term effects unless follow-up is continuous and frequent. For long-term effects, traditional experiments are prone to confounding factors and often struggle to provide reliable results. Field experiments are another viable option, but they're costly and often difficult to replicate. In contrast, synthetic control methods can offer reliable long-term effect estimates without the need for continuous data, but they're prone to confounding. We propose a new approach, synthetic counterfactual regression, which combines the strengths of field experiments and synthetic control methods to provide more accurate long-term effect estimates. Synthetic counterfactual regression can be used in scenarios where some units are treated and others are not, but we've developed an alternative approach that allows us to estimate treatment effects even when all units are treated. Our method can be implemented using a combination of synthetic control methods and various machine learning techniques, making it easy to use in practice. We've tested our method in both simulated and real-world scenarios, and the results show that it outperforms other approaches, including synthetic control methods, in reducing confounding and avoiding selection bias.

To measure the impact of recall bias, a complex probabilistic model is developed. A consistent disease etiology is assumed, with a time sequence from exposure to disease onset. The expression $\beta$ represents the bias in recalling the occurrence of an exposure. It is shown that recalling the timing of both the disease and the exposure involves a time-invariant bias factor, but a time-dependent bias function $B(t)$ that accounts for the bias in recalling the timing of the exposure in relation to the disease onset. Based on these findings, a time-dependent bias function $B(t)$ is proposed to account for the bias in recalling the timing of the exposure. The effect of recall bias on the odds ratio in a case-control study is examined, and it is shown that accounting for the bias in the timing of the exposure can significantly reduce the bias in the odds ratio. Furthermore, it is shown that a time-dependent bias function $B(t)$ can be estimated using a time series of population data and can be used to adjust the biased odds ratio to remove the bias.

We present an alternative variational autoencoder framework based on normalizing flows. Unlike traditional variational autoencoders, which rely on approximate inference techniques, our approach leverages exact inference through the use of normalizing flows. These flow-based models not only excel at learning the posterior distribution of latent variables but also yield more interpretable and efficient inference methods. Specifically, our models allow for exact density estimation of latent positions, eliminating the need for approximate methods like sampling or mean-field approximations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by comparing it to current state-of-the-art variational autoencoders, showcasing its superior performance in terms of both training convergence and testing accuracy. Furthermore, we release a comprehensive set of benchmark tests to facilitate future research in this area.

Urban environments are filled with various sensors, yielding a vast amount of data, often too extensive for manual analysis. 
  This research presents a technique for mining this data using correlated attribute patterns, which can then be applied to urban planning and optimization. 
  We introduce CAMPmine, a system for mining these patterns, based on a mathematical approach that identifies co-occurring patterns in specific contexts. 
  We tested CAMPmine on real-world datasets, examining its performance and accuracy compared to existing methods. 
  Our findings demonstrate the potential benefits and drawbacks of our results to researchers and planners.

This paper explores two novel hybridizable Galerkin methods for highly complex equations, specifically reaction-diffusion and generalized Stokes models. We develop a framework based on a prior work from the 2017 paper (arXiv:1703.10988), adapting it to work with block matrices and applying it to the Stokes equations. We establish that these methods maintain superconvergence for the diffusion solution in the reaction-diffusion case and similarly in the Stokes case for the velocity solution. Furthermore, numerical simulations are provided to validate our findings.

A new method is proposed to conduct sensitivity analysis in the presence of incomplete outcome data, where the analysis is based on a Bayesian framework. The technique employs a Bayesian model to simulate missing outcome data, while utilizing both available and imputed data to inform a joint posterior distribution. This distribution is then used to estimate key parameters, ultimately allowing for the assessment of how different data completion assumptions impact the results. The method is further developed to provide a range of uncertainty estimates and make inferences about parameter space. The method's performance is evaluated through simulation studies and its practical application demonstrated through an analysis of a UK-based primary care study.

In crossover trials with missing gene expression data, a multivariate mixed effects model is proposed where responses from multiple timepoints are analyzed simultaneously. Separate models are fitted for each trial to account for trial-specific variations. An REML method is used to estimate the between-subject variability. Gene-wise non-normality is addressed by using random effect distributional assumptions. For instance, t-distributions can be used to model non-normality if it is known, or neural network algorithms can be employed to learn the distribution of random effects. These learned distributions can then be used in an imputation process. This process involves multiple iterations of modeling and imputation before final analysis. Our simulations show that standard methods of imputation in crossover trials can be improved upon, and suggest that our approach can lead to lower Type I error rates and greater power.

This study addresses the following issue: What does an A_n configuration imply about a given category C when A_n is a special type of algebraic structure defined on 1-C, the one-object categories of C? Our findings reveal that a given C will have an A_n configuration if and only if the stabilization of C, denoted S, possesses a specific property known as the Halpern-Żywinski filtration, thereby connecting the problem to a well-studied filtration structure.

A highly customizable DRAM with adjustable internal clock cycles and bit mask
capabilities now exists. This innovative DRAM, known as PCM-based Programmable DRAM
(PPDRAM), uses a hybrid architecture of SRAM for buffers and PCM for storage cells.
It offers adjustable read margins, written data reliability, and error detection capabilities,
enabling users to adjust DRAM performance to various system demands through
a simple software adjustment. The mechanism of this new DRAM is straightforward:
it adjusts the internal clock cycles and bit mask settings according to user requirements.
The results of simulations show that PPDRAM successfully achieves multiple goals,
such as enhancing DRAM performance, reliability, and error detection capabilities,
while also preserving data integrity.

The introduction of Network Functions Virtualization (NFV) has dramatically altered how networks operate, shifting from hardware-based implementations to software-based functions. This shift has led to increased flexibility and cost-effectiveness but also raises new concerns, such as the security risks associated with software code integrity and malicious software infiltration. To address these security risks, it's essential to develop and employ vulnerability and vulnerability assessment methodologies. This study aims to provide a thorough overview of the latest research on assessing and measuring network function vulnerabilities using data-driven methods.

We investigate the performance and reliability of the conventional surface code with a single type of logical qubit. Current techniques for incorporating additional, non-trivial gates into this code do not significantly improve its fault tolerance. In contrast, we propose a method for promoting the utilization of multi-qubit gates, which is essential for effective error correction, and demonstrate that implementing such gates enables a higher logical operation count. Specifically, we show that utilizing multi-qubit gates enables a higher logical operation count than using single-qubit gates, which in turn enhances the code's fault tolerance. To validate this approach, we utilize a previously developed code-decomposition method and apply it to the surface code with a single type of logical qubit. The results of our simulation, which are based on data obtained from a noisy quantum processor, are promising and hold significant implications for the development of quantum computing hardware.

The OPUS system streamlines analysis and simulation code maintenance by
tracking dependencies, generating automatic benchmarks, and facilitating
benchmark-based validation through a collaborative community effort. Its
extension, OPUS-Bulk, provides a parallel environment for running large batches
of benchmarks, yielding detailed statistical insights. In this contribution, we
demonstrate OPUS-Bulk's capabilities using a series of static equilibrium
simulations run in parallel with OPUS-maintained OpenFOAM, thereby updating its
benchmark database.

A study examining the practical applications of digital game-based learning in an undergraduate engineering course found that participants found the approach engaging and effective in enhancing their understanding of statistical concepts. A control group of students participated in a traditional lecture and workshop format, whereas two treatment groups attended either an in-class workshop or a virtual one using the online platform Discord. Despite the distinct platform used for the virtual workshop, students perceived their learning experience similarly to the control group. Student participants demonstrated improved knowledge compared to a prior group that had not undergone any educational interventions. A positive learning environment, as indicated by increased motivation and a sense of community, was a notable outcome of the educational approach. The outcomes of the study hold significance for hispanic students and those in developing countries, as they highlight the potential of DGBL to bridge the gap in high-quality educational resources.

A recent study on the Martian atmosphere's photochemistry has yielded significant insights into its composition.  The analysis of data from the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, specifically for nitrogen and nitrogen oxide abundance, has provided a comprehensive understanding of nitrogen and molecular oxygen levels.  The findings have allowed for the development of a comprehensive model of the Martian atmosphere's photochemical cycle, which includes the production and destruction of nitrogen and nitrogen oxide species, as well as the formation of molecular and ozone.  The results of this study confirm a seasonal relationship between oxygen and ozone levels, with a significant decrease in ozone levels during springtime due to increased ozone destruction by molecular oxygen.  The study also shows that nitrogen dioxide levels follow a predictable pattern throughout the year, with varying levels of nitrogen dioxide during dust storms, which are a common phenomenon on Mars.  The results of this study align with data from previous orbiters and landers, particularly in regards to the role of molecular oxygen in ozone formation and destruction.  The study also reveals that Martian surface measurements of nitrogen and nitrogen oxide levels can provide valuable information about the Martian upper atmosphere's chemistry.  The results of this study provide a foundation for future research into the Martian atmosphere's chemistry and offer valuable information about the role of Martian surface measurements in understanding the atmosphere's composition and dynamics.

We explore the stability of two-dimensional robust crosscurrents against perturbations within a three-dimensional lattice framework. This involves a system of two quantum fluids, one composed of bosons and the other composed of fermions, interacting via a complex potential that gives rise to a nontrivial geometric current. This current proves resilient against various perturbations, including those affecting its symmetry and the lattice structure, as long as its underlying symmetry is maintained. To analyze its robustness, we utilize a system of two quantum fluids, where one is composed of bosons and the other of fermions, interacting via a complex potential that gives rise to a nontrivial geometric current. This current demonstrates resistance against various perturbations, including those affecting its symmetry and the lattice structure, provided that its underlying symmetry remains intact. By employing a system of two quantum fluids, where one is composed of bosons and the other of fermions, interacting via a complex potential that gives rise to a nontrivial geometric current, we can analyze its robustness. This robustness is characterized through a topological index, which remains invariant under various perturbations, confirming the current's resilience.

MNMT models are trained on multiple languages to enhance low-resource language translation. We examine the effectiveness of MNMT models in low-resource languages, specifically in three under-resourced African languages and four under-resored African and non-African languages. The results show that MNMT models can be successful in low-resource languages if they've been trained on languages that are resource-rich. The models benefit from these training conditions due to the languages sharing similar characteristics. The models also outperform statistical machine translation models. Future work could explore fine-tuning the MNMT models on low-resource languages to improve performance.

A numerical investigation is conducted into the unsteady, nonlinear behavior of plasmas containing dust, using the two-dimensional hydrodynamic model. The study reveals the formation of shock waves for a specific range of parameters, including a critical Mach number and a particular relationship between pressure gradients and electron density variations. The formation of these shock waves drives an instability in the flow, generating oscillations and a large increase in kinetic energy density as the system reaches a state of maximum energy. The oscillations generated by this process continue even after the system reaches maximum energy density, eventually leading to dissipative flow patterns and a gradual decline in kinetic energy density over a prolonged period. A detailed analysis of this process is also carried out, using a simplified model that focuses on the most energetic components of the flow, without accounting for dissipation. The behavior of the flow is found to be similar to that of a Burgers wave, with a specific profile that describes the evolution of energy density over time.

This study focuses on a dense retrieval approach utilizing pre-trained language models that leverage the inherent semantic connections within a corpus's text. A novel architecture is introduced, combining a pre-trained model with a bidirectional encoder-decoder transformer to generate dense embeddings from flat text inputs. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated by achieving top results in retrieval tasks on publicly available datasets, setting a new standard for the field.

Multimodal learning, which combines various types of data to achieve a unified goal, has been a major area of research in machine learning.  Despite existing research in this area, there is still no comprehensive understanding of the various multimodal learning approaches and how they relate to one another. This lack of knowledge makes it difficult for researchers and engineers to choose the right approach for a specific task. This study aims to address this gap by creating a unified framework that ties together various multimodal learning techniques, as well as providing practical guidelines for applying them in real-world situations. By using a hypothetical multimodal learning problem as an example, we illustrate the different approaches and provide readers with a practical understanding of the various multimodal learning techniques.

We investigate the properties of vector and axial vector currents in a relativistic quantum field theory, using massless fermions to simulate vector currents and axial vector currents separately. The behavior of these currents is studied within a framework of one-loop renormalization, where the divergence of the axial current is controlled by a dimension-5 operator that affects its dynamics and its anomalous behavior. The focus of this research is on understanding the behavior of these currents at high orders of a large parameter, such as $1/\Gamma_3$. By examining the behavior of these currents, we identify the leading effects of these currents at high orders of $1/\Gamma_3$ and show that they are described by local expressions that are independent of the gauge field. The results of this research are applied to the properties of a relativistic quantum field theory of electroweak interactions, where the behavior of these currents is used to understand the anomalies in the weak interactions.

In this research, we present a spoken command recognition system based on a tensor-train network framework. The command words are first encoded with a temporal attention-mixture-of-Experts model, where the experts are represented as tensor trains. The resulting feature vectors are then input to a tensor-train network that classifies the commands. We also introduce a method to optimize the tensor trains' factors during training, resulting in a substantial improvement in accuracy for a spoken command recognition task.

This article explores the most recent advancements in quantum-jump methods for analyzing open quantum systems. It includes specific examples of Nelson's Brownian motion, the Sachdev-Kitaev-Kohlbruck model, and the single-molecule method. It also touches on recent experimental realizations, the challenges faced in numerical implementation, and some unresolved or recently resolved paradoxical issues associated with the quantum-jump approach.

The absorption of light by particles is influenced by both the particle's size and its nanoscale characteristics. We have developed a novel theoretical model that builds upon the Maxwell Garnett theory, enabling the prediction of how light interacts with nanoparticles, regardless of their shape. This model, called the Pansari-Penoloponi theory, accounts for the optical properties of both spherical and one-dimensional nanoparticles, such as nanowires and platelets. By utilizing the volume fraction and aspect ratio of these nanoparticles, our model provides a means to estimate their effective electrical conductivity and absorption spectra. The Pansari-Penoloponi theory enables the design of nanoparticle shapes and sizes to enhance light absorption in solar cells, energy harvesting systems, and sensors.

We have developed a new approach to solving first-order logic problems that are computable in polynomial time, where we focus on fixed points as the main decidable element and use them to build a proof framework for our method. This framework is flexible and can be used to build different algorithms for first-order logic problems, including generating algorithms that are based on pushdown automata and indexed languages. Our study shows that fixed points are as powerful as polynomial-time solutions for a wide range of problems, even for those that are non-deterministic. This finding has significant implications for the study of fixed points in both logic and computer science.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks, including speech and language processing. Despite their impressive accuracy, these models are often hindered by their complexity, making it difficult to deploy them on devices with limited resources. In this research, we introduce an innovative LSTM architecture called the Residual LSTM that aims to enhance the performance of existing models while minimizing their size. Our approach is built upon residual connections and a novel technique of inputting multiple future outputs into the LSTM's hidden states. This architecture allows us to design more efficient models that match or even surpass the performance of standard LSTMs. We also propose a residual variant of the LSTM called the Residual Basic LSTM (RB-LSTM) that is specifically designed to optimize the performance of the basic LSTM. Our experiments demonstrate that the new models outperform the baseline models and achieve state-of-the-art results in several benchmark tasks.

This paper examines MAVLink security concerns and presents findings from assessing
official drone firmware security. Leveraging a standard MAVLink connection, we
conduct controlled attacks and demonstrate their impact. The resulting data is used
to validate MAVLink's weak security features, including unencrypted data and
unauthenticated commands. The research also explores potential countermeasures to
mitigate these vulnerabilities.

Understanding network behavior is crucial for creating high-performing distributed systems. Existing research has developed comprehensive network models based on real-world data, but they often overlook the benefits of using such models. in the form of pre-compiled network patterns that can be utilized directly by developers. We introduce Network Navigator, a tool that enables developers to identify suitable network patterns for their applications and incorporate these patterns into their code. We developed a new, efficient pattern representation and a library of common network patterns that can be easily applied across various network contexts. We also created a visual tool, PatternFind, allowing developers to browse available patterns and apply them in their own network environments.

The Maxwell equations in a four-dimensional vacuum, when expressed through a null hyperbolic metric, conform to Einstein's vacuum equations for a specific type of self-dual electric field. This hyperbolic metric is a complex, three-dimensional manifold, and solutions to both sets of equations are closely linked. This approach, inspired by the work of Geroch and Hecht, has been used to classify all solutions up to a certain level of complexity, known as type I. These solutions can be seen as a complex version of the Kerr-NUNZIO spacetimes, and solutions of type II can be derived from type I solutions with additional changes that can be repeated an infinite number of times. Additionally, all self-dual electric fields can be seen as being generated by a complex, three-dimensional hyperbolic space, with electric field lines corresponding to geodesics within this space. This complex space is a three-dimensional submanifold within a larger space, with an additional set of non-constant complex coordinates, and solutions to Maxwell's equations can be derived from complex structures within this larger space.

We're leveraging cosmic muons to visualise hidden tunnels beneath the world's first large-scale salt dome, at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in USA. By utilizing a 1 kt detector made of plasticine-like plastic, we've created a detailed map of the salt formation's shape using muon rays that passed through. These muon rays were tracked using 1,000 photodetectors arranged in five layers, and triggered events with a frequency of 20 Hz. By combining data from various layers, we've created a three-dimensional image of the salt formation's shape, which reveals a large void that spans across 32 meters.

This study presents an updated framework for parsing expression grammars with added features for managing ambiguity through selective and prioritized choice, as well as the application of negative conditions. These enhancements are essential for creating regular and safety specifications in the context of F-14, a framework for formal verification. The existing principles of parsing expression grammars remain unchanged. The presented issues are from the author's personal experience integrating these extensions into the K framework, a verification tool utilized in formal verification.

In this research, we explore the thermal properties of the advanced Cherenkov radiation phenomenon. Specifically, we examine its thermal behavior, thermal scaling, thermal limit, thermal impact on related processes, thermal influence on scattering patterns, and also discuss the thermal scaling of the associated Casimir effect. Our findings indicate that a Cherenkov process' thermal scaling hinges on the involved particles' masses, and that a Cherenkov process' thermal limit is reached when the temperatures exceed certain critical values, derived from the masses of the particles involved. Furthermore, we discuss the thermal effects on related processes, and then analyze how the thermal influence modifies the quantum regime of the scattering patterns. Lastly, we discuss the thermal scaling of the associated Casimir effect.

During language processing, the brain exhibits a unique, complex pattern of electrical activity that can be influenced by the words and concepts we're trying to comprehend, but the neural signals' organization is not influenced by the meaning of what we're reading, according to recent research using high-density electroencephalography. This study investigates whether advanced language models can capture these neural characteristics by comparing their predictions to those of a straightforward model. The investigation revealed that the advanced models were not superior in accurately fitting EEG data when compared to the simpler model. Moreover, the findings indicate that the advanced models' predictions were less effective in distinguishing between words with similar meanings, which may be due to the models' failure to capture subtle linguistic nuances.

Estimating 3D object poses from a single view is a crucial task in robotics and automation. Historically, researchers have relied on synthetic data or existing datasets collected in artificial environments. However, studies have shown that models trained on these sources struggle to generalize in real-world scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we present the first large-scale benchmark for single-view 3D object pose estimation using real-world videos recorded in natural environments. Our findings reveal that in-the-wild training data not only outperforms synthetic data but also existing datasets in a new environment. Moreover, we demonstrate that in-the-wild data can outperform its counterparts in its own environment. Our work sets the stage for using real-world videos to improve 3D object pose estimation. To facilitate further research, we release the in-vil-OMNI dataset and implementation details online at a related website.

In semiconductor-superconductor heterostructures, nonlocal transport through Andreev bound states is a significant phenomenon that facilitates the manipulation of Majorana bound states. Our study examines how these states behave when interacting with a nearby topological insulator or ferromagnet, influencing their electrical properties. Our findings show that topological insulators can generate Andreev reflection in normal-superconductor-nontopological insulator structures. Moreover, the introduction of a ferromagnet in proximity to a superconductor can cause spin-dependent scattering in Andreev bound states. This effect can lead to an imbalance between the probabilities of even and odd parity Andreev bound states, which could be beneficial for detecting and isolating Majorana bound states.

Magnetic reconnection is a widespread phenomenon in highly dynamic astrophysical environments, accelerating particles in various settings such as the solar corona and galaxy centers.  Our study examines the fundamental properties of reconnection in a three-dimensional environment, where a complex magnetic structure interacts with a primary magnetic field.  Our findings indicate that the reconnection process in this scenario is asymmetrical and driven by the movement of magnetic reconnections along curved magnetic lines.  Our analysis also shows that the accelerated particles exhibit a bias towards one direction due to their connection with these curved magnetic lines.  Our results are further supported by three-dimensional simulations of reconnection.  Our conclusions also have relevance for the study of stellar atmospheres and the behavior of energetic particles in magnetospheres.

We calculate one-loop corrections to Higgsstrahlung in models with expanded scalar sectors. This process is particularly relevant in certain types of new physics models. While it's possible to use dimensionally-regulated perturbation theory to calculate the corrections, this approach can be very complex. Instead, we propose a new method that combines partial fractioning and momentum subtraction. This approach can be used to calculate a wide range of one-loop corrections in extended scalar sector models.
A formula for the subdifferential of the joint numerical radius is developed and utilized to investigate the best approximation problems associated with this quantity.

As a surge in data-driven finance has led to an explosion of financial data, deep learning has emerged as a key driver for innovation in the financial sector. However, the increasing adoption of deep learning frameworks without thorough consideration of privacy and security risks poses a significant challenge to businesses. This paper outlines the requirements for building trustworthy financial deep learning systems and presents a novel framework for constructing financial deep learning systems that prioritize both privacy and security. Furthermore, we apply our framework to the field of financial trading, providing a case study on developing a trustworthy quantitative trading platform. The results demonstrate that our approach ensures the confidentiality of financial information and protects it from unauthorized access.

This research explores the link between second-order stochastic mappings and associated Hilbert spaces via an approach rooted in reproducing kernel theory. Within this framework, we develop a framework for representing solutions to stochastic PDEs through a combination of parametric and variational methods, and establish a theoretical underpinning for stochastic multilevel Monte Carlo algorithms through the lens of multivariate vector-valued reproducing kernels.

Our research examines the ignition dynamics of high-pressure hydrogen-oxygen mixtures driven by radio-frequency energy, with a particular focus on the role of seed electrons in the ignition process. We have developed a mathematical model that accurately describes the ignition dynamics, taking into account the experimental constraints and confirming the significance of seed electrons in the ignition of H2-O2 mixtures at high pressures.

We introduce a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BASNet) designed to optimize image segmentation by identifying and following object boundaries within images. This approach is based on a framework that incorporates a segmentation map, a control mask, and a direction map to guide the segmentation process. Within BASNet, an encoder-decoder structure is used in conjunction with a self-referential learning mechanism, which relies on the control mask to localize objects within images. In turn, the direction map enables a directional loss that refines the control mask and guides the final segmentation result. This approach is supported by a boundary-aware loss function that ensures the segmentation map aligns with the object boundaries. We evaluate BASNet through comparative experiments across multiple datasets, including MS COCO, PASCAL VOC 2012, and Cityscapes, and demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art results.

The rapid advancement in communication technology has led to the integration of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technology into connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs). CAVS utilize V2X communication to gather vital information about their surroundings and enhance situational awareness. However, the effectiveness of this technology is heavily dependent on the type of network used, including its connectivity and availability. Mobile edge computing (MEC) has emerged as a viable solution to improve network connectivity and reduce the burden on resource-constrained CAVs. This study examines the benefits of MEC in V2X networks, specifically focusing on the use of MEC servers to process and analyze environmental data. A novel framework is proposed to enable MEC servers to provide real-time guidance to CAVs, while maintaining confidentiality. The proposed framework is evaluated using a case study on the impact of weather conditions on driving. Simulation results demonstrate the potential of MEC servers to provide accurate and timely advice to CAVs. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of MEC servers on the driving behavior of CAVs and identifies the optimal configuration for this specific application.

Our investigation involves examining the behavior of active Brownian particles that interact with a solid boundary, specifically considering the influence of a nearby passive system. Each ABP is influenced by a discrete set of preferred interactions, represented by $\kappa$ vectors, and is driven by a force in the direction of these vectors. By analyzing this model, we can understand how the ABP system evolves as it approaches inactivity, and how the combined system responds to changes in its active properties using a measure of the system's activity. Near rigid boundaries, the ABP system tends to cluster and create a counter-rotating flow that is influenced by the proximity to the boundary, with a stronger flow observed when closer to the boundary. However, in a passive system, the ABP particles can become trapped in a stable state, creating a stable flow that is influenced by the activity of the ABP system and the Rouse length. By analyzing the behavior of the ABP system in relation to the passive system, we can identify a characteristic characteristic characteristic characteristic (CCC), which is a measure of the system's behavior in a specific active state.

A novel method has been developed to accurately calculate electronic states in plasmas by employing the Siegert states concept. Unlike traditional models that define states as bound particles within a box, the Siegert states represent the electronic configuration of atoms in an ionized gas environment. By applying this method to helium ions, researchers have determined the energies of these states and their transitions. The calculated results are consistent with previous studies and experimental findings, providing a comprehensive understanding of atomic processes in plasmas. The Siegert states have significant implications for the analysis of ionized gases and other plasma phenomena.

These changes occurred simultaneously with intense bursts of nonthermal X-rays and with significant plasma heating. The observed changes are highly periodic with a 75-second period, and their amplitudes are significant, reaching 20% for intensity and 20 km/s for velocity. In this presentation, I'll examine how a certain term affects quantum chromodynamics when acting across great distances, utilizing a lattice structure.  The presence of this term causes color fields to become confined, resulting in the deuterium-like formation of $P$ and $P_c$ states.  Our research utilizes the HISQ action, employing multiple lattice spacings and volumes, to study the effects of this topological term.  The findings indicate that the zero modes cause the system to be highly sensitive to volume, leading to a need for renormalization of the relevant term matrix element.  The outcome of this process reveals that the system is in a stable state, with the formation energy of $P$ and $P_c$ states matching previous theoretical predictions.  Our research paves the way for future studies of other exotic hadrons, such as those with hidden charm or heavier quark masses.

A theoretical model has been developed to determine the angle at which a swift ion can penetrate through solid boundaries without experiencing reflection. The model uses a simple, easy-to-compute formula that takes into account the ion's velocity, surface irregularities, and thermal movement. Theoretical calculations using this model were applied to various ions (lead, carbon, and deuterium) at different energies (up to 30 MeV) and observed a decrease in the angle prediction with increasing ion velocity and surface roughness. The calculated angles were then compared with experimental results from ion-beam analysis and showed a reasonable match within the studied energy range.

The article presents an anti-plagiarism solution for source code, utilizing hash function-based and meta-data encryption techniques, making the source code and its hash values inaccessible without the decryption key. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, securing the source code and its hash values, thus preventing unauthorized modifications to the latter, at the index time, thus ensuring the integrity of the system.

We consider the Dirichlet series F(s) with a real s and real part greater than 0, and we define a modified version F_{\lambda}(s) equal to the product of λ and F(s), where λ is a constant greater than 0. Assuming that F(s) has a specific form with a degree d and a specific type of pole at s equal to 0, we establish that there exists a specific value N depending on λ, F, and d such that F_{λ}(s) is equal to λ to the power of d for all real s less than the value N.

We define a $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup $G$ as a metric group $(G,d)$ that has a subgroup $H$ with $k$ generators, where $d(x,y)\geq 1$ and $d(h,k)\geq 1$ for all distinct elements, and $d(h,k)<1+\epsilon$ for all elements, where $h,k\in G$. The study reveals that if the metric group $(G,d)$ is a $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroup with a large size and certain properties, then it must be isometric to a group with a specific expansion.

In nonparametric statistics, estimating log-concave densities is a fundamental problem that has significant applications, particularly in statistical inference of Dirichlet process mixture models. Recent breakthroughs have led to the development of highly influential and widely-used non-convex optimization methods for this task. However, these approaches often result in subpar density estimates due to their propensity for producing inaccurate and computationally challenging results. Our research introduces a novel, non-convex estimator for log-conconave densities based on a Gaussian process framework. By leveraging the concept of Bayesian optimization, we create a nonparametric Bayesian basis that enables efficient and accurate density estimates. Our proposed estimator consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple performance metrics and real-world applications.

We utilize the Wang-Landau algorithm to generate a non-equilibrium ensemble of configurations in one-dimensional granular systems that are out of equilibrium and find stationary and non-stationary states that are stable or unstable. The simulation results for the average densities at these states match well with previously numerical findings and theoretical predictions from the theory of granular gases. We also demonstrate that our method can be used to sample configurations in stable states resulting from inelastic collision dynamics, which are known to be challenging to access.

In the context of a two-player game called Explorer-Distributor, a researcher with limited resources must navigate to a target city, which is determined by a random target city chosen from a set, which in turn is chosen by the researcher. The researcher's goal is to identify the target city, while the distributor's objective is to minimize their entropic uncertainty about it. This game can be seen as a model for collaborative research in fields like physics, which involves a researcher trying to reach a 'truth', and a distributor representing a community of experts who aim to decrease their uncertainty about it through peer review. This study shows that the distributor's optimal strategy involves setting a threshold for their entropic uncertainty, such that if it is below this threshold, they are certain of the correct answer. This strategy also involves a'shock-absorbing' principle, which is based on a concept introduced by physicist and philosopher David H. Freedman. The study also shows that if the distributor's initial uncertainty is already low, then the distributor's optimal strategy involves accurately guessing the correct answer. This study also introduces a new concept called'shock-absorbing' peer review and provides a mathematical formula for it.

The Brownian motion and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process are widely applied in image processing, signal processing, and communication technologies. The autocovariance or even autocorrelation plays a significant role in these applications. The focus of this research lies in deriving precise analytical expressions for the variance and the frequency-frequency correlation of these processes, expressed in terms of the first and second-order moments of the driving white Gaussian noise. The derived formulas can be used in scenarios where the variance of this noise is not significantly small.

In this paper, we propose a new solution method that can generate one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional wave solutions for the higher-order Broer-Kaup system and its variants. Using this approach, we derive novel exact solutions and confirm that it is applicable to other nonlinear systems due to the universal nature of its constraints.

Inspired by the works of I. L. Frez Gallego, M. G. Gerver and V. M. Vinogradredev on the conservation of energy in the incompressible Euler equation under localized vorticity control and R. Abgrall on the limitations of Lagrangian methods for conservation laws, we have investigated both theoretical and numerical aspects of energy conservation for the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equation under the condition that vorticity is confined to a specific area. A novel Lagrangian approach that incorporates elements of Lagrangian and Eulerian methods was developed, which was then compared with existing Eulerian methods. The comparison showed that Eulerian methods generally fail to produce accurate results, as seen in the table of relative errors of energy conservation for the rotating vortex and the Gaussian hill problems, which demonstrated that our new method provided superior accuracy.

VIRUP is a C++ open source tool that allows users to interact with massive scientific datasets stored on a file system.  This program is optimized for high performance on Linux systems with virtual reality technology to provide an immersive experience.  It is designed to be accessible through a web interface, enabling users to interact with the data without needing to learn the program's features.  This web-based interface offers additional safety measures to prevent accidental data modifications.  This document outlines the design and functionality of the VIRUP user application, which provides an interactive visual representation of the dataset by loading a dataset into memory and projecting it into a 3D format.  This 3D format is then continuously updated as the user naviges the dataset through space and time to provide a seamless and low-latency experience.  To achieve this seamless experience, VIRUP utilizes a technique known as prediction, which anticipates the user's movement requests and loads the necessary data before the user makes the request.  This technique is made possible through the use of asynchronous threading, which allows the program to work on multiple tasks at once.  This parallel processing is achieved through the use of asynchronous threading, which allows the program to work on multiple tasks at once.  To further enhance the user experience, VIRUP provides a number of features that allow the user to manipulate the dataset in a more intuitive way, such as rotating the 3D representation of the dataset in real-time.  This manipulation allows the user to visualize the dataset

The Data Bricks Space Mission is a hands-on learning activity grounded in data
physicalization, developed to help kids aged 10-12 understand data principles.
Drawing on research and drawing inspiration from LEGO bricks, the activity
transforms data representation into tangible, scene-oriented models using
Lego bricks as physical objects, Lego vehicles, and a space mission narrative.
Data is visualized as physical locations on a planet, while the bricks serve as
data points, and the movement and color of the vehicles represent data changes
and values over time, making data education engaging for both students and
educators. Early trials of the mission have taken place in schools and at a data
science workshop, yielding valuable insights that will inform future iteration and
refinement.

In a software-defined networking environment, network operators need to identify the actual paths that data is taking to diagnose issues and manage performance. Since network configurations can differ from what is planned and a single packet can travel differently than another, there are specific requirements to identify active paths accurately using flow monitoring. We present a method for determining the active paths of flows in a network by analyzing data collected from various monitoring points. Our approach uses a model that captures the possible paths that data is taking and identifies the most likely active paths based on data we have. We show that to ensure accurate identification, there are certain requirements that must be met, including the presence of at least one path that is active, and the accurate identification of all possible paths that are active, and we also show that our approach has the lowest possible false dismissal rate and false alarm rate compared to other similar approaches.

Enforcing disentanglement in neural representations is complicated due to factors like overlapping feature vectors and non-linear relationships between dependent representations. A new approach addresses this issue by developing a method to align disentangled representations with their corresponding ground truths, resulting in a more effective disentanglement technique. This technique involves training a model to generate latent vectors based on the disentangled representation and relevant input variables while keeping the non-relevant input variables constant. Empirical evidence from various benchmarks demonstrates that this approach results in more disentangled representations compared to existing models. Furthermore, by utilizing disentangled representations, our method showcases promising prospects for unsupervised transfer learning.

This research examines the influence of hydrokinetic energy extraction from a two-foil tandem configuration on various scales, with a focus on the scale factor's effect on power output and the optimal foil spacing. To achieve this, we utilized the open-source framework MFEM for solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in both two and three dimensions, with a particular emphasis on the two-dimensional model's ability to replicate the three-dimensional model's wake dynamics through a modified interface. The research compares the one-dimensional wake model to the full three-dimensional model, as well as to a simplified model that accounts for the foil configuration in a two-dimensional setting. The results indicate that, for a given tandem configuration, the foil spacing that yields the maximum energy harvest is found to be dependent on the scale factor, with a direct relationship observed between spacing and the scale factor.

This article examines the theoretical and computational aspects of Bayesian inference in extracting spectral functions from lattice QCD simulations. The discussion delves into the underlying Bayesian framework, its connection to the maximum entropy approach, and an alternative regularization method called evidence decay. It also touches on the use of a technique called the Gibbs sampling algorithm without delving into the technical aspects, and it looks at the modern applications of Bayesian inference beyond spectral extraction. Finally, the article shares its own perspective on the field and offers concluding thoughts and recommendations for further research.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that measures the spin dependence of the tunneling rates. Our experiment involved creating two types of Andreev spectroscopy plots based on whether an external magnetic field aligned the spin of the quantum dot or not. By analyzing the difference in the plots, we were able to directly measure the spin-dependent tunneling rates. Our findings show that the charge tunneling is highly sensitive to the spin state of the quantum dot, which makes our method a reliable way to detect spin-dependent tunneling.

The central objective in the field of drug discovery is to identify suitable molecular targets involved in specific diseases, allowing researchers to develop effective treatments. With advancements in high-throughput experimental technologies and bioinformatics resources, numerous publicly accessible databases have been created to store information on target identification. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of these databases, highlighting their capabilities and how they contribute to the understanding of target-based diseases, while also exploring the challenges and limitations that remain in the field. The review will focus on utilizing existing databases to understand the role of target-based approaches in the treatment of various diseases, with a particular emphasis on the impact of genomic variations on drug targets. The discussion will also cover the application of computational methods in the selection of target-based drug interventions, with a focus on the development of predictive models that leverage experimental data to identify effective targets. The review will conclude by outlining future directions for research in the field of precision medicine and personalized therapy.

This text evaluates implementation strategies in the context of lambda-calculus, 
focusing on topological space models. We examine and compare the key attributes 
of these models using different strategies and give preference to those that can be 
defined locally within the models themselves. We then apply our preferred 
approach to create a simple model of lambda calculus based on topological space 
structures.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) are
perioidically interacting galaxies.  Observations of the SMC's tidal debris
toward SMC indicate that a significant portion of the neutral gas in the SMC
remains in a state of constant interaction with the LMC.  We have conducted a
comprehensive 1.4 GHz continuum and neutral gas survey of the SMC's most
southern region, which is approximately 1 degree square.  We have used the
Mopra telescope to survey the SMC's most southern region, which is
incorporated into the LMC's tidal debris zone.  We have found 11 new HI clouds
in the SMC with masses of 5,000 to 10,000 solar masses.  We have found that
these clouds are experiencing a range of velocities, which is indicative of
the SMC's interaction with the LMC.  We have found that the SMC is composed of a
series of discrete, cloud-like structures that are distributed in a manner
consistent with the LMC's interaction.  We have found that the LMC and SMC are
currently in the early stages of a collisional event, which is estimated to
happen in approximately 200 million years.  We have found that the LMC and SMC

Advanced smart grid technology has made it possible to track electricity usage in real-time, enabling utilities to monitor and address any unusual activity. A novel approach to detecting electricity theft in smart grids utilizes a deep recurrent neural network that's trained on time-series data from advanced metering infrastructure. Our results show that this method outperforms traditional energy-based detection methods, accurately identifying irregularities even when data quality is compromised. When tested with synthetic electricity theft patterns, the method accurately detected 95% of incidents during the initial stage and 90% in real-time data. To further improve performance, we developed a second model that analyzes both historical and live data, resulting in a detection rate of 95%.

Our research focuses on understanding the characteristics of the tight surface graphs that arise from the three-vertex link, which is the most basic type of link on a torus. We have developed a precise mathematical expression to calculate the crossing numbers of these graphs, taking into account their size. We have also determined new limitations for the maximum number of non-overlapping regions that these graphs can have, which expands our current understanding in this area and confirms a previously proposed theory. Furthermore, our work on finding the smallest tight surface links for small sizes provides a foundation for future research into tighter links, which is an ongoing challenge that remains unsolved.

Researchers have made the first direct observation of the Ωc0 baryon in decay processes involving a proton and a kaon. Data from experiments conducted at the LHC using 3 fb−1 of proton-proton collision data at 7 and 8 TeV energies are used to determine the Ωc0 baryon's mass and lifetime. Specifically, its mass is calculated as 2666.5 ± 0.5 ± 1.0 MeV/c2 and its lifetime is measured as 150 ± 50 ± 25 ± 7 fs. The first and third error values come from statistical and systematic uncertainties, respectively, while the second value represents a modeling-related uncertainty.

In the field of remote sensing, unsupervised learning is crucial, and we focus on a particular category, subspace clustering, which is a type of unsupervised learning. Subspace clustering methods, such as K-SClique, is an L1-regularized technique that identifies sparse and dense clusters, but its efficiency is hindered by its computationally expensive optimization problem. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel solver that employs an adaptive step size based on the sub-gradient, allowing for efficient subspace clustering. Experimental results demonstrate that our solver provides the best clustering results in a timely manner.

The thermal conductivity and albedo of Arctic sea ice are influenced by the vertical and horizontal distribution of brine. Changes in the depth and shape of the brine within the sea ice affect how heat is transferred and how much sunlight it reflects. This research examines the relationship between the microstructure of sea ice and its thermal conductivity and albedo by using X-ray computed tomography scans of 12 different samples. Each sample was then analyzed under different conditions to simulate how brine would move within it over time. Two methods were used to track the movement of brine: one that assumes it moves uniformly, and another that assumes it moves vertically due to the differences in density between the ice and the air above. By using these assumptions, researchers were able to create a range of possible values for the brine's thermal conductivity and albedo. These ranges can then be applied to real-world scenarios to estimate the thermal conductivity and albedo of Arctic sea ice.

Our study reveals that the final stages of ultracold collisions between atoms and heavier molecules can be precisely created through the strategic application of magnetic fields over time. This process is made possible by the Stueckelberg interferometric technique, which leverages the quantum nature of the lighter scattering particle relative to the heavier target to control the interaction. Notably, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the difference in magnetic moment between the lighter and heavier particles, thereby enabling the control of scattering results even in the presence of identical quasibound states.

We extend the concept of nonequilibrium dynamics from the realm of nonextensive thermostatistics to higher dimensions of phase space. This is achieved by modifying the Kullback-Leibler relative entropy such that it is based on the hyper-Kullback-Leibler divergence. This new concept of entropy, denoted as S, naturally adheres to the fundamental laws of thermodynamics. We demonstrate that the stationary state of this modified entropy is characterized by the Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution, which reduces to the conventional Kullback-Leibler entropy when the phase space is one-dimensional. Furthermore, we show that the resulting dynamics of S are equivalent to the superstatistical dynamics of Langevin processes, which are applicable in any dimension of phase space. This connection highlights the fact that the super-Poissonian behavior of Langevin processes is a natural outcome of the extended entropy, rather than being an anomaly.

We have established a theoretical basis for Floquet Weyl semimetal states in a three-dimensional periodic system subjected to a weak and incommensurate driving force. This breakthrough is based on a Weyl node model in a Floquet Hamiltonian, where unique Weyl points are characterized by distinct topological charges. The findings reveal that the Floquet Weyl semimetal exhibits robust and non-linear responses to specific electromagnetic fields. Moreover, the phenomenon of anomalous Floquet insulator emergence is identified as a consequence of a particular Weyl point reaching the boundary of the Brillouin zone. The implications of these discoveries are expected to facilitate the discovery of materials exhibiting these properties.

As processing power is shifted to from servers to user devices, it is essential to develop a computation model that incorporates both. This involves combining both local and remote computation, with our proposed solution being LoDAC, a decentralized computation protocol that enables user devices to perform tasks on-site and then submit them for verification and compensation. LoDAC utilizes a novel consensus mechanism that incorporates proof-of-stake, randomization, and a fairness mechanism to mitigate the risks of bias. Through our analysis, it is demonstrated that LoDAC is secure against various attacks and efficient in its use of resources. It also effectively incentivizes users to produce accurate results, with computational fairness being maintained even when the platform is large. Furthermore, LoDAC is shown to be more efficient than the current blockchain-based computation model.

Optimizing rate and distortion in video coding is a complex task, particularly for 3D point clouds, due to their irregular encoding schemes. Since point cloud decoding typically involves a hierarchical structure, balancing rate and distortion is often achieved by evaluating performance across different levels, rather than just the last one. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on a single level of distortion, our research proposes an innovative optimization technique based on a two-stage learning approach that takes into account the performance of all levels simultaneously. We develop a hierarchical neural network to predict the distortion of various levels, based on the encoding process of the point cloud. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving better performance than current point cloud coding methods, particularly under low-bitrate conditions.

The QCD phase diagrams for two and three flavors of quarks are compared and matched based on lattice simulations, yielding a new, more precise alignment method between the two diagrams. This method successfully aligns key features, such as the boundaries of the chiral and deconfinement transitions, and aligns with prior results from chiral perturbation theory. The new approach provides an independent method for matching the two diagrams, which is desirable given existing discrepancies between lattice simulations and perturbation theory. The obtained alignment allows for a unified understanding of the QCD phase diagrams for strong interaction phenomena.

Recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning (SSL) have led to impressive results in unsupervised transfer learning, outperforming traditional hand-crafted features for medical imaging classification tasks. Despite these advances, the lack of ground truth labels in certain medical imaging applications remains a significant obstacle to leveraging SSL. A novel framework called Confusing Autoencoder (Confenformer), which utilizes multi-view autoencoders to generate pseudo labels for unlabeled data, has been proposed. By learning representations from diverse perspectives, the Confenformer can accurately label a majority of the data. Empirical evidence from both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates the Confenformer's ability to achieve comparable results to supervised learning methods, using only a minimal amount of labeled data.

A new area of research, few-shot font generation, has emerged as a faster and more efficient method compared to creating each font character individually. Most current techniques employ a single embedding space for characters and glyphs. We propose the Font Embedding Space Clustering (FESC) framework, which utilizes a multi-space embedding model to group related font characters across different spaces. FESC starts by embedding each component of a Latin character in a shared space, then clusters similar components together. It also enables the transfer of learning between different space assignments. We introduce a new method to predict the space assignment of an unseen character based on a small set of examples, and show that it outperforms existing techniques that rely on randomly assigned initial font embeddings.
